The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends a document (writing that people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or meeting notes) to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it. Advice that the person will act on by themselves, right away, in the code they are working on is not meant for other people, so Claude does not need to publish it.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. Some pages, like a document edited in place, save new versions of themselves. Such a save reaches this session like any other republish, as a notice on a watched artifact or a conflict on Claude's next publish, and Claude then re-reads the page, merges the changes and republishes.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. Claude refuses whether it wrote the page or the person supplied it, and whatever purpose is claimed, such as a prop or a test, when the page would work as the real thing. If publishing is refused, Claude does not suggest other ways to host or share the page.

action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

41	## High: the `seq_resume` hand-off and the hub
42	
43	These three come from the same change: on every connect, storage now sends the hub an 8 B `seq_resume` reply, and DESIGN.md says "the hub continues from the next value". They decide the hub's design, so they should be settled in the PR before the hub is written.
44	
45	### PF-01: The hub can't stamp `seq` when a message arrives [Both docs] [Breaks plan]
46	- **Sensor-Pipeline.md** (*Decisions*, "Hop 2 … carries the 24 B on-disk record", 2026-10-23): the hub stamps `seq` and the µs time and builds the whole record, CRC included, as each message arrives; the record then waits in the 1024-record queue. `include/hub.h` matches: `gt_hub_accept(h, msg, now_us, gt_record *out)` returns a finished record.
47	- **DESIGN.md:** the hub stamps `seq`; the hub queue is "1024 records × 24 B"; Mechanism E requires that processes "tolerate unavailable peers during startup".
48	- **What breaks:** a hub that has just started doesn't know its `seq` until storage replies. If storage is down or still recovering when the hub starts, which Mechanism E says must be tolerated, `gt_hub_accept` can't fill `seq` and so can't compute the CRC. The hub must either stop taking sensor messages (breaking Mechanism E) or queue records without a `seq` and stamp `seq` + CRC at send time, which changes `hub.h`, what the queue holds, and DESIGN.md's "records" wording.
49	- **Still possible:** the timestamp can still be taken on arrival, so a queued record keeps its real receive time.
50	- **Resolution (decided 2026-10-26, docs only):**
51	  - **The rule:** the hub stamps the time on arrival, and `seq` + CRC just before `send()`. The 1024-record queue holds records without `seq` or CRC, and a `seq` is used only when `send()` returns OK.
52	  - **Where it's written:**
53	    - Sensor-Pipeline.md: the new *Hub contract (hop 2)* section, a Decisions bullet, an amendment note on the 2026-10-23 hop-2 Decision, and the *Later* bullets.
54	    - DESIGN.md: both Hub → storage rows, the hub-queue budget row, and *At what rate*.
55	  - **Still to do:** rewrite the `gt_hub_accept` comment in `include/hub.h` when the hub steps start.
56	
57	### PF-02: The hop-2 sender can't reuse the `ipc_sock` seam [Breaks plan]
58	- **Sensor-Pipeline.md** (*Later*): the sender "reuses the `ipc_sock` seam to send 24 B records".
59	- **The seam can't receive:** `gt_sock_ops` has only `connect`, `send`, `disconnect` and `destroy` ([include/ipc_sock.h:19-32](include/ipc_sock.h#L19-L32)).
60	- **What `seq_resume` needs:** a `recv` op; a third state between connecting and sending ("connected, waiting for the reply"), where the plan's state machine (*IPC client: connection and ring rules*) has only DISCONNECTED and CONNECTED; and a rule for a reply that never comes, without blocking (`storage_feed` simply waits up to 2 s). `tests/fake_sock.h` would need the same additions.
61	- **DESIGN.md** documents the reply, so it is consistent here; Sensor-Pipeline.md is not.
62	- **Resolution (decided 2026-10-26, docs only):**
63	  - **The seam:** `gt_sock_ops` gains a non-blocking `recv` op. It returns 0 bytes when nothing is waiting and `GT_ERR_IO` when the peer has closed.
64	  - **The sender:** it gets an `AWAITING_RESUME` state between DISCONNECTED and SENDING, and sends nothing until the reply arrives. A reply that doesn't come within 2 s, or a bad one, means disconnect and retry with backoff.
65	  - **Where it's written:** in Sensor-Pipeline.md's *Hub contract (hop 2)*: the state diagram, the API sketch (`hub_sender.h`), the `fake_sock.h` additions and the reserved test prefixes (`HSO`, `HSR`, `HSS`, `HSQ`, `HSL`).
66	  - **Still to do:** the header, fake and sender, test first.

68	### PF-03: A storage `kill -9` loses records with no trace in the log [Both docs]
69	- **Sensor-Pipeline.md** treats every loss as visible: "whichever component refuses a reading records the gap"; a message lost in transit shows up as "the jump in the counter" (`sensor_seq_gap`); ladder rung 4 requires the data counters plus `gap.value` to "cover every counter".
70	- **DESIGN.md:** the row "Storage killed (`kill -9` or OOM) with an unsynced batch" promises one GAP record covering the lost range (`recovery_gap`), and the Evaluation plan counts lost readings as "seqs the hub sent − seqs committed − seqs covered by a GAP record".
71	- **What breaks:** this PR changed the hand-off to "storage replies with its last **accepted** `seq` … and the hub continues from the next value". After a `kill -9`, the accepted-but-unsynced records are gone, so the reply is the last `seq` on disk. A hub that continues from there reuses the lost records' `seq`s: no hole appears, no GAP is written, and the hub's sent list holds the same `seq` twice, so the Evaluation plan's formula no longer works.
72	- **The code disagrees with itself:** the header comment in [src/storage_feed_main.c:11-12](src/storage_feed_main.c#L11-L12) says the next records "start a recovery_gap", but the code sends from `resume + 1` ([src/storage_feed_main.c:73](src/storage_feed_main.c#L73)), so it never does. `storage_faults.sh`'s check that "the reply equals the last `seq` on disk" passes precisely because the loss isn't marked.
73	- **Proposed fix (a DESIGN.md decision):** a hub that is still running keeps its own counter, so storage sees the hole and writes the GAP; only a freshly started hub uses `resume + 1`. In short, the next `seq` is the larger of the hub's own next `seq` and `resume + 1`.
74	- **Resolution (decided 2026-10-26, docs only): the proposed fix was adopted.**
75	  - **The rule:** next `seq` = max(own next, `resume + 1`), where the hub's own counter is 1 + the last `seq` whose `send()` succeeded.
76	  - **Storage needs no change:** `gt_seq_check` already returns GAP for a hole, and `recovery_gap` is logged.
77	  - **DESIGN.md:**
78	    - The hub row states the max rule.
79	    - The Storage-killed row no longer says "no GAP record". It names the cases with no GAP: the hub restarted too (shown by `unclean_shutdown` only), or the log was empty.
80	    - The `has_last` field says only a fresh hub starts at 0.
81	    - The Evaluation plan's lost-readings formula is marked exact within one hub run. Power pulls use the "loss ≤ 1 batch" target instead.
82	  - **Sensor-Pipeline.md:** a new Decision (with the rejected alternative), plus the Mechanism D *Not done yet* bullet.
83	  - **The rule is shared:** a pure `gt_next_seq` in `storage_proto.h`, called by both the hub's sender and `storage_feed`, so the fault rounds test the hub's own numbering code.
84	  - **Done (with PF-04/05, 2026-10-26):**
85	    - `gt_next_seq` written test first (NSQ 8/8, red then green).
86	    - `storage_feed` uses it, its header comment is fixed, and its new `-r` mode keeps its counter across storage restarts.
87	    - `storage_faults.sh` runs one feed across all rounds. In `kill9 50`, each of the 50 kills left exactly one GAP, written at the next start (round *n* showed `gaps=n−1`, and the settle start added the 50th; 5493 readings covered). The final check found sent = committed + GAP-covered.
88	  - **Still to do:** the hub's hop-2 sender calls `gt_next_seq` (PF-02's sender steps).

90	## Tooling bugs
91	
92	### PF-04: `storage_faults.sh` fails every round (confirmed by a run)
93	A run of `tools/storage_faults.sh sigterm 2` in WSL:
94	
95	```
96	FAIL round 1: expected an empty-log reply, got:
97	FAIL round 2: expected seq_resume last=59, got:
98	storage_faults: 2 sigterm rounds, 2 failed checks
99	```
100	
101	Storage itself was correct: the feed's output file later held `seq_resume: last=59, sending from 60`, and the round log showed `storage_stop clean=1` with no `unclean_shutdown`.
102	- **Cause:** `storage_feed` prints with `printf`, and stdout redirected to a file is fully buffered until the program exits. The script reads the file after `sleep 0.2` ([tools/storage_faults.sh:97-98](tools/storage_faults.sh#L97-L98)), before the line has been written.
103	- **Fix:** `setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IOLBF, 0)` (line buffering) or an `fflush(stdout)` after the reply line in `storage_feed`, then re-run `sigterm 20` and `kill9 50`. The PR's status table marks these runs "Not recorded", which is accurate.
104	- **Resolution (2026-10-26):**
105	  - `storage_feed` sets line buffering first thing in `main`. A smoke run showed the reply line in the output file while the feed was still running.
106	  - The script no longer sleeps a fixed time. It waits up to 5 s for the round's `seq_resume:` line.
107	  - **Also found while fixing it:** a `kill -9` leaves the old socket file behind, so the old "wait for the socket" step returned before the new storage had recovered. The script now waits for storage's `storage_start` log line.
108	  - **Results:** `sigterm 20` gave 0 failed checks: 1773 sent, 1773 committed, 0 GAP readings. `kill9 50` is under PF-05.
109	
110	### PF-05: `kill9` rounds verify the log before recovery has run (plausible)
111	- `log_verify` runs right after the kill, before the next start's recovery ([tools/storage_faults.sh:116-117](tools/storage_faults.sh#L116-L117)).
112	- A SIGKILL can cut a large `pwrite` short, leaving a partial tail. DESIGN.md allows that, because recovery truncates it, and its target is "0 corrupt records accepted **after restart**". The verifier would still report `partial_tail` as a failure.
113	- **Fix:** in `kill9` mode, start and stop storage once (so recovery runs) before verifying, or verify at the start of the next round.
114	- **Resolution (2026-10-26):**
115	  - **The recovery pass:** each `kill9` round now pauses the feed, starts storage once so it recovers (it must log `unclean_shutdown`), SIGTERMs it (it must log `storage_stop clean=1`), and only then runs `log_verify`.
116	  - **Also found while fixing it:** the old 0.1–0.9 s kill delay always landed before storage's 1 s flusher tick. A trial run showed `data=0` in every round with 0 failed checks: nothing was ever committed, every loss hit the empty-log case (no GAP), and torn-tail recovery was never exercised. The `kill9` delay is now a random 1.0–2.9 s, so kills land anywhere in the flush cycle.
117	  - **Results:** `kill9 50` gave 0 failed checks and `corrupt_files=0` in every round: 18742 sent = 13249 committed + 5493 GAP-covered.
118	  - **Not shown:** whether any of the 50 recoveries actually cut a torn tail (`records_removed > 0`). The script deletes its work directory after a passing run, so that evidence wasn't kept.
119	
120	## Contradicts DESIGN.md (storage)
121	
122	### PF-06: Records from the end of a day go into the next day's segment
123	- **DESIGN.md:** "one segment file per UTC day".
124	- `gt_flusher_tick` rolls over to the new day's segment *before* it flushes ([src/storage_server.c:212-228](src/storage_server.c#L212-L228)), and `gt_storage_rollover` doesn't flush first. Up to about 60 s of records received before midnight are written into the new day's file.
125	- **Fix:** flush (or attempt to) before switching segments.
126	- **Resolution (2026-10-26):** the fix was adopted.
127	  - **The change:** `gt_storage_rollover` flushes pending records into the old segment before creating the new one, and its events are passed on. If that flush fails, the existing degraded path cuts the old tail and the records go into the new segment.
128	  - **Remaining limit:** records that arrive between midnight and the flusher's next pass (≤ 1 s) still go into the old day's file. This is now written in DESIGN.md.
129	  - **Tests:** SRO-13 and SRO-14 are new. SRO-11, SRO-12 and FTK-05 were changed with approval, because they asserted the old behaviour; each kept its scenario. All were seen red, then green.
130	
131	### PF-07: A storage-made GAP record carries the gap's end time
132	- **DESIGN.md** record table: a GAP's timestamp is the "gap start"; "a gap ends at the timestamp of the next DATA record".
133	- `gt_seq_gap_record` uses the incoming record's timestamp ([src/storage_seq.c:42](src/storage_seq.c#L42)), so start and end come out identical and the gap's length is lost. Its `seq` (the first refused reading) and `value` are correct.
134	- **Resolution (2026-10-26):**
135	  - **The rule:** a storage-made GAP is stamped with the last accepted record's time, the earliest the gap could have started.
136	  - **After a restart:** recovery reports the newest record's time (`last_timestamp_us` in `gt_scan_result`, `gt_recover_report` and `gt_storage_open_info`), so a GAP found after a `kill -9` gets it too.
137	  - **Signature change:** `gt_seq_gap_record` gained a `last_accepted_us` argument.
138	  - **Tests:** RSC-10, SRV-11, SOP-13 and SFL-11 are new, and SBL-03 gained a timestamp check. SQG-07 and SFL-03 were changed with approval, because they asserted the end time. All were seen red, then green (322 tests).
139	  - **Real process:** in a manual `kill -9` run, the GAP for seqs 372–458 carried record 371's time, and the next record showed it lasted 1.063 s. `storage_faults.sh kill9 5` and `sigterm 3` still gave 0 failed checks.
140	
141	### PF-08: Commits are not logged and fsync is not timed
142	- **DESIGN.md**, Mechanism D: "Every commit logged with count and duration; report fsync p50/p99". The `fsync_slow` row: "fsync duration measured on every commit; log any fsync over 1 s".
143	- `gt_storage_flush` reports no event on success and doesn't time the fsync, so neither row can be measured.
144	- **Resolution (2026-10-27):**
145	  - **Timing inside storage:** an optional monotonic clock (`gt_storage_set_clock`) times every commit, write + fsync (`commit_us`) and the fsync alone (`fsync_us`). That includes the rollover pre-flush and the shutdown flush. `gt_storage_stats` gains `commits`, `last_commit_records`, `last_commit_us` and `last_fsync_us`.
146	  - **Logging:** `gt_storage_log_commit` logs `storage_commit records=N commit_us=T fsync_us=F` at INFO, then `fsync_slow fsync_us=F records=N` at WARN for an fsync over 1 s. The flush thread calls it once per pass, and `storage_main` around the final shutdown.
147	  - **p50/p99:** worked out offline from the `storage_commit` lines (decided 2026-10-27), so no state is kept in the process.
148	  - **Tests:** SFL-12 to SFL-15, FTK-07 and FTK-08 are new. FTK-02 was changed with approval: it asserted that a healthy flush logs nothing. All were seen red, then green.
149	  - **WSL check:** a 3 s run at 200 Hz logged four commits (fsync 4.6–7.7 ms) whose records add up to the 612 committed.
150	
151	### PF-09: DESIGN.md describes disk-full and read-only handling as done
152	- The `storage_disk_full` row (`ENOSPC`, `statvfs`, the 64 KB reserve) and the `storage_readonly` row (`EROFS`) read as built. Nothing in `src/` mentions `statvfs`, `ENOSPC` or `EROFS`; a full card shows up only as `storage_write_error` + `storage_degraded`.
153	- Lucas's *Not done yet (Mechanism D)* list says so. DESIGN.md should mark both rows as planned until they land.
154	- **Resolution (2026-10-26, docs only):**
155	  - **Disk-full row:** ENOSPC / `statvfs` and `storage_disk_full` are marked planned. The built parts (backlog at 50/75/90%, refuse and count when the buffer is full, the GAP on recovery) are left as they were.
156	  - **Read-only row:** marked `Storage (planned)`, matching the *Analysis (planned)* rows.
157	  - **Today's behaviour is stated in both rows:** a full card or EROFS shows as `storage_write_error` (or `fsync_error`, or `segment_create_error` at rollover) + `storage_degraded`, with the records kept in memory.
158	  - ***With what retention*:** the disk-full steps and the 64 KB reserve are marked planned too.
159	  - **Still to do:** the handling itself, which needs a "disk full" status out of the file seam first (Lucas's *Not done yet*).
160	
161	### PF-10: Storage heartbeat: not built, and DESIGN.md disagrees with itself
162	- The architecture diagram has the **flush thread** send a 1 Hz heartbeat to `sup.sock`; the `fsync_slow` row says the **rx thread** sends it (so a stalled fsync can't stop it).
163	- Neither is built; `storage_main.c` says it "arrives with Mechanism E". DESIGN.md needs one answer before it is.
164	- **Resolution (proposed 2026-10-27, docs only; pending Lucas):**
165	  - **The proposal:** the **rx thread** sends it, as the `fsync_slow` row already said. The flush thread can sit in a stalled `fsync()`, so a heartbeat from it would stop exactly when the supervisor needs to tell "slow" from "hung".
166	  - **Where it's written:** DESIGN.md's diagram arrow now runs from the rx thread to `sup.sock`. Sensor-Pipeline.md has a Mechanism D Decisions bullet marked *pending Lucas*, and its *Not done yet* points to it.
167	  - **What building it needs:** `gt_storage_serve`'s `poll()` gets a 1000 ms timeout instead of `-1`, and `gt_storage_stats` gains the time the current flush started (the beat carries "flush in progress since t" and the committed count).
168	  - **Still to do:** Lucas confirms it, then it is built with `sup.sock` (Mechanism E).
169	
170	### PF-11: The (N, T) batching experiment can't run as specified
171	- **DESIGN.md**, Mechanism D: compare fsync count, latency and CPU at (N, T) = (1, 1 s), (64, 10 s) and (64, 60 s).
172	- N and T are compile-time `#define`s, and the flush thread checks only once a second ([src/storage_server.c:26](src/storage_server.c#L26)), so N = 1 can't mean one fsync per record, and the N = 64 trigger can be up to 1 s late.
173	- **Resolution (2026-10-27):**
174	  - **Run-time N and T:** `storage_main -n N -t T_SECONDS` (N 1..43,690, T 1 s..1 day; default 64 / 60 s) sets them through the new `gt_storage_set_batch` → `gt_pending_set_limits`. `storage_start` logs `batch_n` / `batch_t_s`. The `#define`s stay as the defaults, so no existing test changed.
175	  - **The flusher is woken at N:** between its 1 s passes, `gt_flusher_run` waits in the new `gt_storage_wait_due` on a condition variable (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC` on Linux) instead of sleeping. The append that makes a flush due wakes it, so N = 1 is one fsync per record and N = 64 is no longer up to 1 s late. T, rollover and the clock checks stay on the 1 s pass. On stop, `storage_main` calls the new `gt_storage_wake`.
176	  - **Two changes from the plan:**
177	    - **Signal on "becomes due", used once.** The plan said a wait returns while pending ≥ N. That would make the flusher spin after a failed flush, because the records stay pending. Now the signal fires only when an append turns a flush from not due to due, and each wait uses it up (SWT-03).
178	    - **The two cross-thread tests also check timing.** The plan said they would check return values only, but a wait that ignored the wake would still return 1 at its 2 s timeout. SWT-04/05 therefore also check the wait ended in under 1.5 s.
179	  - **Tests, written first:**
180	    - `PNL` (`tests/test_pending_limits.c`, 5 cases);
181	    - `SBT` (`tests/test_storage_batch.c`, 4 cases);
182	    - `SWT` (`tests/test_storage_wait.c`, 6 cases, two of them on a real second thread).
183	
184	    PNL replaced the plan's "defaults equal the `#define`s" case, which PND-05/06 already cover.
185	  - **Docs:** DESIGN.md *How writes are batched* (the options and the wake) and the Evaluation plan's (N, T) line; Sensor-Pipeline.md's Mechanism D Code map, a Decisions bullet, the three prefixes and a verification step.
186	  - **Still to do:**
187	    - The real-process check: `storage_main -n 1 -t 1` with `storage_feed SOCK 50 10` should log about 50 `storage_commit records=1` lines.
188	    - The (N, T) experiment itself, on the Pi.

190	### PF-12: The verifier doesn't compare against the hub's sent `seq`s
191	- **DESIGN.md**, Test tooling: the verifier "then compares the log against the hub's sent-sequence log".
192	- `log_verify` checks every CRC, that `seq` strictly increases across segments, and that every hole is covered by a GAP, but there is no hub yet to compare against. Together with PF-03, a `kill -9` loss is currently undetectable.
193	- **Resolution (2026-10-27):**
194	  - **The rule:** compare ranges, not a per-`seq` log. Within one hub run the sent `seq`s are one unbroken range A..B: a `seq` is used only when `send()` succeeds, and a running hub's counter stays ahead of storage's reply (PF-03). A passing report already guarantees every `seq` from its first to its last is stored or GAP-covered, so:
195	    - lost = the sent `seq`s outside that range (`sent_seq_lost`);
196	    - a `seq` after B fails as `seq_not_sent`;
197	    - `seq`s before A are earlier hub runs and are allowed.
198	  - **Changed from the plan:** checking `data + gap_readings = B − A + 1` was dropped. It only held because `storage_feed` never sends a GAP. A hub GAP has its own `seq`, and its value counts refused readings that never got a `seq`, so the sum would break once the hub exists.
199	  - **The code:**
200	    - `gt_verify_sent` in `log_verify.h` / `log_verify.c`, written test first (VSR-01 to VSR-07 in `tests/test_verify_sent.c`).
201	    - `log_verify [--sent A..B] DIR` prints `sent=N lost=L` and fails on a mismatch.
202	    - `storage_faults.sh`'s settle check uses it in place of the bash arithmetic. It still checks N = B − A + 1 (no `seq` reused) and that the log starts at A, since its log starts empty.
203	  - **Docs:** DESIGN.md *Test tooling → Verifier*; Sensor-Pipeline.md's Mechanism D Code map, a Decisions bullet, the `VSR` prefix and the settle-check description.
204	  - **Tests:** `make test`, `make asan` and `make memcheck` all pass with VSR included (2026-10-27).
205	  - **Still to do:**
206	    - Record a `storage_faults.sh sigterm` / `kill9` run with the new check.
207	    - The hub logs its own sent range when it stops (hub step H8), so the same flag works on the Pi.

209	### PF-13: `clock_unsynced` / `clock_synced` are never logged
210	- **DESIGN.md**, System clock row: log the unsynced period with `clock_unsynced` / `clock_synced`.
211	- `storage_main`'s `clock_synced()` is sound (a 2026-10-01 floor plus `adjtimex`, which returned TIME_OK in WSL), but only `retention_skipped` is logged, once per unsynced spell.
212	- **Resolution (2026-10-27):**
213	  - **The events:** the flush thread now logs `clock_unsynced` at WARN on the first unsynced pass of a spell (including the very first pass), and `clock_synced unsynced_ms=N` at INFO on the first synced pass after it. N comes from the monotonic clock. A clock that is synced from the start logs neither. `retention_skipped` is unchanged.
214	  - **Tests:** FTK-09, FTK-10 and FTK-11 are new. FTK-09 and FTK-10 were seen red, then green. FTK-11 is the "stays quiet" guard, so it passed from the start.

217	- `storage_stop` lacks the segment and last `seq` that DESIGN.md's new text says it carries.
218	- `storage_backlog` doesn't say which threshold (50/75/90%) was crossed.
219	- Only the newest segment's recovery is logged, so an older segment truncated during the walk back for the last `seq` goes unreported.
220	- **Resolution (2026-10-27):**
221	  - **`storage_stop`:** DESIGN.md never actually said what this line carries, so the first point's premise was wrong. It was still adopted (decided 2026-10-27): `storage_stop` now has `segment=… last_seq=…` like `storage_start`. The segment comes from the new `gt_storage_active_segment` (SRO-15).
222	  - **`storage_backlog`:** it now carries `percent=N pending=P`. The new `gt_storage_log_rx_events` (SLE-01 to SLE-04) does this, and the rx loop uses it.
223	  - **The walk back:** the open info now lists each older segment that recovery cut or renamed (up to 8 by name, any more counted), and `storage_main` logs each as `recovery_event` / `segment_corrupt` (SOP-14, SOP-15). The walk back can rename segments as well as cut them, which the finding didn't mention.
224	  - **Tests:** all new tests were seen red, then green (SLE-04 is a NULL-safety guard and passed from the start).
225	  - **WSL check:** with yesterday's segment ending in 10 torn bytes and today's header-only, storage logged `recovery_event segment=log-20261026.bin bytes_removed=10 records_removed=1` at WARN, and `storage_stop` showed `segment=log-20261027.bin last_seq=4`.

227	### PF-15: Doc errors
228	- **[Both docs]** The Hub range-check row says "light 0–65535 **lux**". Sensor-Pipeline.md says "Raw counts are stored, never lux", and its Step 7 changed this row to "raw count". Git history shows the fix was lost in merge #71 (`complete-pipe` → `main`), not by Lucas.
229	- The Storage "malformed message" row says `gt_msg_decode()` detects it; storage actually uses `gt_record_decode`.
230	- **Resolution (2026-10-26):**
231	  - **Range-check row:** the Hub row reads "light raw count 0–65535" again, the wording Sensor-Pipeline.md's Step 7 had put in. Sensor-Pipeline.md itself already said raw counts, so only DESIGN.md changed.

237	- **Sensor-Pipeline.md** (*Design principle*): "`src/ipc_sock.c` is the only file that makes socket system calls"; everything else goes through `gt_sock_ops` so tests can use a fake.

239	- `storage_server.c` calls `accept`, `recv` and `send` directly ([src/storage_server.c:79](src/storage_server.c#L79), [96](src/storage_server.c#L96), [115](src/storage_server.c#L115)), so its loop is tested only over real sockets (SSV), not with a fake. Defensible for a server, but it should be recorded as a Decision.
240	- **Resolution (2026-10-27, docs only):**
241	  - **The rule:** the socket seam is for clients. Servers (`listen_sock.c`, `storage_server.c`, and later the hub's rx loop) call the socket API directly and are tested over real sockets (LBD, SSV, and later the hub loopback). A server-side seam with its own fake was rejected: an ops table and a second fake to test very little logic.
242	  - **Where it's written:** a new Sensor-Pipeline.md Decisions bullet; the *Design principle → IPC seam* bullet now says "client-side"; so does the header comment in `include/ipc_sock.h`.

245	- **Sensor-Pipeline.md**: "Update the Status section only at the end of the day, when asked." The PR rewrites Lily's *Not done yet* bullet to say "**The storage process itself is done**".
246	- Lucas's own *Not done yet (Mechanism D)* still lists disk full, read-only filesystem, the heartbeat, and the fault and power-pull runs.
247	- The file's opening paragraph still scopes it to "the 24 B record the hub sends to storage", but it now ends with a second top-level section with its own Status, *Not done yet* and Log, so "update Status" no longer says which one.
248	- **Resolution (2026-10-27):**
249	  - **The overclaim:** the *Not done yet* bullet now says the storage process "is built and passes its WSL fault rounds". It names what is still open (disk full, read-only, heartbeat, on-Pi power pulls) and points to Mechanism D's own list.
250	  - **The opening paragraph:** it now says the file has a second part, *Mechanism D: storage*, and names both Status sections. The rule applies to either: update only at the end of the day, when asked.

254	- **Sensor-Pipeline.md** (*Decisions → Log sink deferred*): where log lines go is to be decided together with the light process.
255	- `storage_main` writes to stderr ([src/storage_main.c:68-75](src/storage_main.c#L68-L75)). A reasonable choice, but it now sets the precedent for every process.
256	- **Resolution (2026-10-27, docs only):**
257	  - **The rule:** stderr for every process, adopted as a joint decision. Children inherit the supervisor's stderr, so under systemd every line reaches the journal. A shared file sink (rotation becomes our problem) and the monitor process (waits on Mechanism E) were rejected.
258	  - **Where it's written:** Sensor-Pipeline.md's *Log sink* Decision (was *Log sink deferred*), plus its *Later* and *Not done yet* bullets for `light_sensor_main.c`; one sentence in DESIGN.md's log-format paragraph.
259	  - **No code change:** `storage_main` already does this.

261	### PF-19: The Code map is out of date
262	- The diagram still shows the storage process as not built (☐).
263	- The "storage rx thread" row says `gt_record_decode → gt_storage_append(gt_record)`; `gt_storage_append` now takes the raw 24 B and decodes them itself, and `gt_storage_open` has a new signature.
264	- **Resolution (2026-10-27):**
265	  - **The diagram:** the storage process is marked built (`storage_main.c`, with `gt_storage_serve` as the rx loop, and `storage.c` doing append with decode and the seq guard, flush, fsync and rollover). The hub's `gt_hub_accept` box now says it stamps µs only, with `seq` and CRC added at send (PF-01).
266	  - ***Who calls whom*:** new rows for `gt_storage_open` (wrapping `gt_storage_open_ops`), `gt_storage_append` (raw 24 B + `now_ms`, with its OK / CORRUPT / FULL results), the flush thread's rollover-then-flush, and the hub sender's `gt_next_seq` + encode.

268	## Smaller storage edge cases
269	
270	### PF-20
271	- **`.corrupt` files:** retention never deletes them, a second `.corrupt` of the same name silently replaces the first (`renameat`), and once the directory holds 128 names (`GT_FILE_LIST_MAX`), `gt_storage_open` fails.
272	- **Rollover failure logs every second:** while a new segment can't be created, `segment_create_error` is logged on every 1 s tick.
273	- **The 1970 file:** a Pi that boots with no network time and an empty log writes `log-19700101.bin` until NTP syncs (acknowledged in Lucas's *Not done yet*).
274	- **Resolution (2026-10-27):**
275	  - **Unique `.corrupt` names:** a second `.corrupt` copy of the same segment no longer replaces the first. Recovery picks the first free name of `<name>.corrupt`, `<name>.2.corrupt` … `<name>.99.corrupt` (SRV-12). Every name still ends in `.corrupt`, so `log_verify` counts them.
276	  - **Retention and the 128-name limit:** `.corrupt` files are still never deleted (decided 2026-10-27: they are evidence). The limit is now documented in `storage.h` and DESIGN.md: more than 128 names stops storage at start with `storage_open_error`, and the fix is to clear old `.corrupt` files by hand.
277	  - **`segment_create_error`:** it is now logged once per failure spell, and the next successful rollover re-arms it (FTK-12).
278	  - **The 1970 file (decided 2026-10-27):** on an empty log with an unsynced clock, `storage_main` now waits up to 120 s for the clock before open names the first segment. It logs `clock_wait max_s=120`, then `clock_wait_done waited_s=N synced=0|1`. The hub's 1024-record queue covers the wait. "Empty log" comes from the new `gt_storage_log_empty` / `_ops`, which uses the same listing open uses (SOP-16, red then green).
279	  - **Still possible:** with no network for the whole 120 s, it still starts a 1970 file. That stays a documented limit in `storage.h` and DESIGN.md.
280	  - **Not tested yet:** the wait itself has not been seen running, because WSL's clock is always synced. It needs a check on the Pi with the network unplugged.
281	  - **Doc follow-up (2026-10-27):** Sensor-Pipeline.md's *Not done yet (Mechanism D)* still listed "the 1970 file" as unfixed, saying a proper fix meant `storage_main` waiting for the clock. That wait now exists, so the bullet was reworded to the open item: the on-Pi check of the clock wait.
282	
283	## What meets the plans
284	
285	**DESIGN.md**
286	- **`storage_main.c` start-up order:** the one-listener lock, then recovery, then bind `storage.sock`, then the flush thread, then the rx loop. A second copy refuses to start.
287	- **Shutdown:** on SIGTERM, storage takes any records already in the socket, joins the flush thread, does the final flush, and writes the clean-shutdown marker only if that flush succeeded. The stop signals are blocked in the flush thread, SIGPIPE is ignored, and the exit status is honest. Seen working in the PF-04 run.
288	- **Recovery:** marker check, newest-segment header check and `.corrupt` rename, scan to the first bad record (magic, type, version, CRC, `seq`, partial tail), truncate + fsync, then the walk back for the last `seq`.
289	- **Durability:** fsync per batch; directory fsync when a segment is created; on a failed write or fsync the batch stays pending, storage is marked degraded, and the next cycle truncates to the last committed offset before rewriting.
290	- **Backlog and refusals:** `storage_backlog` at 50/75/90%; when full, refuse and count while still reading the socket; the next accepted record brings a GAP whose `seq` is the first refused reading.
291	- **Retention:** 30 days, deleting only outside the window and beyond the newest 30 segments; skipped while the clock is unsynced.
292	- **Locking:** the mutex is never held during file I/O.
293	- **Documentation brought in line:** the single pending buffer and memory budget, the commit sequence, recovery step 5, the retention rule, `storage.sock` as `SOCK_SEQPACKET`, and the `seq_resume` layout.
294	- **Verifier:** read-only, checks `seq` order across segment boundaries, its GAP rule matches what append writes, and it counts `.corrupt` files without failing on them (VFY, 10 tests).
295	- **Logging:** every line goes through `gt_log_format` with µs wall-clock timestamps.
296	
297	**Sensor-Pipeline.md**
298	- **Lock helper:** the one-listener lock moved into a shared `src/` helper (`listen_sock.c`) with `fork()`-based tests (LCK), exactly as *Decisions* planned. `hub_listen` behaves as before.
299	- **Hop 2:** the 24 B record is checked with `gt_record_decode` and appended as the raw bytes received, per the 2026-10-23 decision. A storage GAP uses `sensor_id 0`, which the wire-format section allows.
300	- **Wrong-length frames:** storage receives into a 25 B buffer and closes the connection on a wrong length (`ipc_bad_message`), mirroring the hub's 17 B rule.
301	- **Same patterns:** events returned rather than logged, time passed in, a file seam with a fake for tests, `MSG_NOSIGNAL`, `SOCK_SEQPACKET`.
302	- **Test ID prefixes:** none of the 23 new prefixes collide with the existing ones.
303	
304	## Recommended before merge
305	
306	1. ~~**Decide PF-01 to PF-03 in DESIGN.md:** the hub stamps the timestamp on arrival and `seq` + CRC at send time; the socket seam gains a `recv` op and the sender a "waiting for `seq_resume`" state; a running hub keeps its own `seq` counter. Update Sensor-Pipeline.md's *Decisions* and `include/hub.h` to match.~~ **Done in both documents (2026-10-26).** `include/hub.h` waits for the hub steps.
307	2. ~~**Fix PF-04** (and PF-05), then run `storage_faults.sh sigterm 20` and `kill9 50` and record the results.~~ **Done (2026-10-26):** both ran with 0 failed checks; results are in PF-04/05 and the Mechanism D Status table.
308	3. ~~**Fix or document PF-06 and PF-07.**~~ **Done (2026-10-26):** both fixed test-first; see their Resolution lines.
309	4. ~~**Mark PF-09's rows as planned**~~ (done 2026-10-26) and settle PF-10's heartbeat owner thread. **Proposed (2026-10-27):** the rx thread, written into both documents and marked pending Lucas, who owns the heartbeat.
