# Pipeline Findings

Adversarial review of branch `Menu-Mechanism-D` (Lucas's Mechanism D storage work) against `DESIGN.md` and `Sensor-Pipeline.md`, before it merges to `main`. Reviewed 2026-10-26 at commit `7741f69`, covering every change since the `main` merge `d9344f3`.

**How it was checked:** every new or changed file in `src/`, plus `tools/storage_faults.sh` and the `DESIGN.md` / `Sensor-Pipeline.md` edits, was read line by line. No code was changed. `storage_main`, `storage_feed` and `log_verify` were built into a scratch directory, and `tools/storage_faults.sh sigterm 2` was run once in WSL (see PF-04).

**Labels:**
- **[Both docs]:** contradicts `Sensor-Pipeline.md` *and* `DESIGN.md`.
- **[Breaks plan]:** a change that stops something `Sensor-Pipeline.md` intends from working as planned.
- **Confirmed:** shown by reading the code and, where noted, by running it. **Plausible:** follows from the code but not seen happening.

## Summary

| ID | Finding | Contradicts | Severity | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PF-01 | The hub can't stamp `seq` when a message arrives | [Both docs] [Breaks plan] | High | Decided in docs; hub not built |
| PF-02 | The hop-2 sender can't reuse the `ipc_sock` seam | Sensor-Pipeline.md [Breaks plan] | High | Decided in docs; seam not changed |
| PF-03 | A storage `kill -9` loses records with no trace in the log | [Both docs] | High | Decided in docs; `gt_next_seq`, `storage_feed` and the fault rounds follow it; hub sender not built |
| PF-04 | `storage_faults.sh` fails every round | Tooling (confirmed by a run) | High | Resolved (2026-10-26) |
| PF-05 | `kill9` rounds verify the log before recovery has run | Tooling (plausible) | Medium | Resolved (2026-10-26) |
| PF-06 | Records from the end of a day go into the next day's segment | DESIGN.md | Medium | Resolved (2026-10-26) |
| PF-07 | A storage-made GAP record carries the gap's end time | DESIGN.md | Medium | Resolved (2026-10-26) |
| PF-08 | Commits are not logged and fsync is not timed | DESIGN.md (2 rows) | Medium | Resolved (2026-10-27) |
| PF-09 | DESIGN.md describes disk-full and read-only handling as done | DESIGN.md | Medium | Resolved in docs (2026-10-26); handling not built |
| PF-10 | Storage heartbeat: not built, and DESIGN.md disagrees with itself | DESIGN.md | Medium | Proposed in docs (2026-10-27); pending Lucas |
| PF-11 | The (N, T) batching experiment can't run as specified | DESIGN.md | Low | Resolved (2026-10-27); the experiment itself is not run yet |
| PF-12 | The verifier doesn't compare against the hub's sent `seq`s | DESIGN.md | Low | Resolved (2026-10-27); the hub's sent-range line comes with the hub |
| PF-13 | `clock_unsynced` / `clock_synced` are never logged | DESIGN.md | Low | Resolved (2026-10-27) |
| PF-14 | Some log lines are missing their `key=value` fields | DESIGN.md | Low | Resolved (2026-10-27) |
| PF-15 | Doc errors: "lux" range check, wrong decode function | [Both docs] / DESIGN.md | Low | Resolved (2026-10-26) |
| PF-16 | Socket calls outside `src/ipc_sock.c` | Sensor-Pipeline.md | Low | Resolved in docs (2026-10-27) |
| PF-17 | Lily's Status section edited; "storage is done" overclaims | Sensor-Pipeline.md | Low | Resolved (2026-10-27) |
| PF-18 | The log sink was chosen by one side | Sensor-Pipeline.md | Low | Resolved in docs (2026-10-27) |
| PF-19 | The Code map is out of date | Sensor-Pipeline.md | Low | Resolved (2026-10-27) |
| PF-20 | Smaller storage edge cases | DESIGN.md | Low | Resolved (2026-10-27); the 1970 wait still needs an on-Pi check |

Resolved since the first pass: `storage_main.c` now exists, `seq_resume` is documented in DESIGN.md, and DESIGN.md's memory budget now matches the single pending buffer (see *What meets the plans*).

**Progress (2026-10-26):** PF-01 to PF-03 are settled on paper in both documents. Each finding below has a **Resolution** line saying what was decided and what is still to do. Later the same day, PF-04 and PF-05 were fixed in code, PF-03's rule was built as `gt_next_seq` and used by `storage_feed`, and `sigterm 20` and `kill9 50` were run with 0 failed checks. Storage itself was not changed.

## High: the `seq_resume` hand-off and the hub

These three come from the same change: on every connect, storage now sends the hub an 8 B `seq_resume` reply, and DESIGN.md says "the hub continues from the next value". They decide the hub's design, so they should be settled in the PR before the hub is written.

### PF-01: The hub can't stamp `seq` when a message arrives [Both docs] [Breaks plan]
- **Sensor-Pipeline.md** (*Decisions*, "Hop 2 … carries the 24 B on-disk record", 2026-10-23): the hub stamps `seq` and the µs time and builds the whole record, CRC included, as each message arrives; the record then waits in the 1024-record queue. `include/hub.h` matches: `gt_hub_accept(h, msg, now_us, gt_record *out)` returns a finished record.
- **DESIGN.md:** the hub stamps `seq`; the hub queue is "1024 records × 24 B"; Mechanism E requires that processes "tolerate unavailable peers during startup".
- **What breaks:** a hub that has just started doesn't know its `seq` until storage replies. If storage is down or still recovering when the hub starts, which Mechanism E says must be tolerated, `gt_hub_accept` can't fill `seq` and so can't compute the CRC. The hub must either stop taking sensor messages (breaking Mechanism E) or queue records without a `seq` and stamp `seq` + CRC at send time, which changes `hub.h`, what the queue holds, and DESIGN.md's "records" wording.
- **Still possible:** the timestamp can still be taken on arrival, so a queued record keeps its real receive time.
- **Resolution (decided 2026-10-26, docs only):**
  - **The rule:** the hub stamps the time on arrival, and `seq` + CRC just before `send()`. The 1024-record queue holds records without `seq` or CRC, and a `seq` is used only when `send()` returns OK.
  - **Where it's written:**
    - Sensor-Pipeline.md: the new *Hub contract (hop 2)* section, a Decisions bullet, an amendment note on the 2026-10-23 hop-2 Decision, and the *Later* bullets.
    - DESIGN.md: both Hub → storage rows, the hub-queue budget row, and *At what rate*.
  - **Still to do:** rewrite the `gt_hub_accept` comment in `include/hub.h` when the hub steps start.

### PF-02: The hop-2 sender can't reuse the `ipc_sock` seam [Breaks plan]
- **Sensor-Pipeline.md** (*Later*): the sender "reuses the `ipc_sock` seam to send 24 B records".
- **The seam can't receive:** `gt_sock_ops` has only `connect`, `send`, `disconnect` and `destroy` ([include/ipc_sock.h:19-32](include/ipc_sock.h#L19-L32)).
- **What `seq_resume` needs:** a `recv` op; a third state between connecting and sending ("connected, waiting for the reply"), where the plan's state machine (*IPC client: connection and ring rules*) has only DISCONNECTED and CONNECTED; and a rule for a reply that never comes, without blocking (`storage_feed` simply waits up to 2 s). `tests/fake_sock.h` would need the same additions.
- **DESIGN.md** documents the reply, so it is consistent here; Sensor-Pipeline.md is not.
- **Resolution (decided 2026-10-26, docs only):**
  - **The seam:** `gt_sock_ops` gains a non-blocking `recv` op. It returns 0 bytes when nothing is waiting and `GT_ERR_IO` when the peer has closed.
  - **The sender:** it gets an `AWAITING_RESUME` state between DISCONNECTED and SENDING, and sends nothing until the reply arrives. A reply that doesn't come within 2 s, or a bad one, means disconnect and retry with backoff.
  - **Where it's written:** in Sensor-Pipeline.md's *Hub contract (hop 2)*: the state diagram, the API sketch (`hub_sender.h`), the `fake_sock.h` additions and the reserved test prefixes (`HSO`, `HSR`, `HSS`, `HSQ`, `HSL`).
  - **Still to do:** the header, fake and sender, test first.

### PF-03: A storage `kill -9` loses records with no trace in the log [Both docs]
- **Sensor-Pipeline.md** treats every loss as visible: "whichever component refuses a reading records the gap"; a message lost in transit shows up as "the jump in the counter" (`sensor_seq_gap`); ladder rung 4 requires the data counters plus `gap.value` to "cover every counter".
- **DESIGN.md:** the row "Storage killed (`kill -9` or OOM) with an unsynced batch" promises one GAP record covering the lost range (`recovery_gap`), and the Evaluation plan counts lost readings as "seqs the hub sent − seqs committed − seqs covered by a GAP record".
- **What breaks:** this PR changed the hand-off to "storage replies with its last **accepted** `seq` … and the hub continues from the next value". After a `kill -9`, the accepted-but-unsynced records are gone, so the reply is the last `seq` on disk. A hub that continues from there reuses the lost records' `seq`s: no hole appears, no GAP is written, and the hub's sent list holds the same `seq` twice, so the Evaluation plan's formula no longer works.
- **The code disagrees with itself:** the header comment in [src/storage_feed_main.c:11-12](src/storage_feed_main.c#L11-L12) says the next records "start a recovery_gap", but the code sends from `resume + 1` ([src/storage_feed_main.c:73](src/storage_feed_main.c#L73)), so it never does. `storage_faults.sh`'s check that "the reply equals the last `seq` on disk" passes precisely because the loss isn't marked.
- **Proposed fix (a DESIGN.md decision):** a hub that is still running keeps its own counter, so storage sees the hole and writes the GAP; only a freshly started hub uses `resume + 1`. In short, the next `seq` is the larger of the hub's own next `seq` and `resume + 1`.
- **Resolution (decided 2026-10-26, docs only): the proposed fix was adopted.**
  - **The rule:** next `seq` = max(own next, `resume + 1`), where the hub's own counter is 1 + the last `seq` whose `send()` succeeded.
  - **Storage needs no change:** `gt_seq_check` already returns GAP for a hole, and `recovery_gap` is logged.
  - **DESIGN.md:**
    - The hub row states the max rule.
    - The Storage-killed row no longer says "no GAP record". It names the cases with no GAP: the hub restarted too (shown by `unclean_shutdown` only), or the log was empty.
    - The `has_last` field says only a fresh hub starts at 0.
    - The Evaluation plan's lost-readings formula is marked exact within one hub run. Power pulls use the "loss ≤ 1 batch" target instead.
  - **Sensor-Pipeline.md:** a new Decision (with the rejected alternative), plus the Mechanism D *Not done yet* bullet.
  - **The rule is shared:** a pure `gt_next_seq` in `storage_proto.h`, called by both the hub's sender and `storage_feed`, so the fault rounds test the hub's own numbering code.
  - **Done (with PF-04/05, 2026-10-26):**
    - `gt_next_seq` written test first (NSQ 8/8, red then green).
    - `storage_feed` uses it, its header comment is fixed, and its new `-r` mode keeps its counter across storage restarts.
    - `storage_faults.sh` runs one feed across all rounds. In `kill9 50`, each of the 50 kills left exactly one GAP, written at the next start (round *n* showed `gaps=n−1`, and the settle start added the 50th; 5493 readings covered). The final check found sent = committed + GAP-covered.
  - **Still to do:** the hub's hop-2 sender calls `gt_next_seq` (PF-02's sender steps).

## Tooling bugs

### PF-04: `storage_faults.sh` fails every round (confirmed by a run)
A run of `tools/storage_faults.sh sigterm 2` in WSL:

```
FAIL round 1: expected an empty-log reply, got:
FAIL round 2: expected seq_resume last=59, got:
storage_faults: 2 sigterm rounds, 2 failed checks
```

Storage itself was correct: the feed's output file later held `seq_resume: last=59, sending from 60`, and the round log showed `storage_stop clean=1` with no `unclean_shutdown`.
- **Cause:** `storage_feed` prints with `printf`, and stdout redirected to a file is fully buffered until the program exits. The script reads the file after `sleep 0.2` ([tools/storage_faults.sh:97-98](tools/storage_faults.sh#L97-L98)), before the line has been written.
- **Fix:** `setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IOLBF, 0)` (line buffering) or an `fflush(stdout)` after the reply line in `storage_feed`, then re-run `sigterm 20` and `kill9 50`. The PR's status table marks these runs "Not recorded", which is accurate.
- **Resolution (2026-10-26):**
  - `storage_feed` sets line buffering first thing in `main`. A smoke run showed the reply line in the output file while the feed was still running.
  - The script no longer sleeps a fixed time. It waits up to 5 s for the round's `seq_resume:` line.
  - **Also found while fixing it:** a `kill -9` leaves the old socket file behind, so the old "wait for the socket" step returned before the new storage had recovered. The script now waits for storage's `storage_start` log line.
  - **Results:** `sigterm 20` gave 0 failed checks: 1773 sent, 1773 committed, 0 GAP readings. `kill9 50` is under PF-05.

### PF-05: `kill9` rounds verify the log before recovery has run (plausible)
- `log_verify` runs right after the kill, before the next start's recovery ([tools/storage_faults.sh:116-117](tools/storage_faults.sh#L116-L117)).
- A SIGKILL can cut a large `pwrite` short, leaving a partial tail. DESIGN.md allows that, because recovery truncates it, and its target is "0 corrupt records accepted **after restart**". The verifier would still report `partial_tail` as a failure.
- **Fix:** in `kill9` mode, start and stop storage once (so recovery runs) before verifying, or verify at the start of the next round.
- **Resolution (2026-10-26):**
  - **The recovery pass:** each `kill9` round now pauses the feed, starts storage once so it recovers (it must log `unclean_shutdown`), SIGTERMs it (it must log `storage_stop clean=1`), and only then runs `log_verify`.
  - **Also found while fixing it:** the old 0.1–0.9 s kill delay always landed before storage's 1 s flusher tick. A trial run showed `data=0` in every round with 0 failed checks: nothing was ever committed, every loss hit the empty-log case (no GAP), and torn-tail recovery was never exercised. The `kill9` delay is now a random 1.0–2.9 s, so kills land anywhere in the flush cycle.
  - **Results:** `kill9 50` gave 0 failed checks and `corrupt_files=0` in every round: 18742 sent = 13249 committed + 5493 GAP-covered.
  - **Not shown:** whether any of the 50 recoveries actually cut a torn tail (`records_removed > 0`). The script deletes its work directory after a passing run, so that evidence wasn't kept.

### PF-06: Records from the end of a day go into the next day's segment
- **DESIGN.md:** "one segment file per UTC day".
- `gt_flusher_tick` rolls over to the new day's segment *before* it flushes ([src/storage_server.c:212-228](src/storage_server.c#L212-L228)), and `gt_storage_rollover` doesn't flush first. Up to about 60 s of records received before midnight are written into the new day's file.
- **Fix:** flush (or attempt to) before switching segments.
- **Resolution (2026-10-26):** the fix was adopted.
  - **The change:** `gt_storage_rollover` flushes pending records into the old segment before creating the new one, and its events are passed on. If that flush fails, the existing degraded path cuts the old tail and the records go into the new segment.
  - **Remaining limit:** records that arrive between midnight and the flusher's next pass (≤ 1 s) still go into the old day's file. This is now written in DESIGN.md.
  - **Tests:** SRO-13 and SRO-14 are new. SRO-11, SRO-12 and FTK-05 were changed with approval, because they asserted the old behaviour; each kept its scenario. All were seen red, then green.

### PF-11: The (N, T) batching experiment can't run as specified
- **DESIGN.md**, Mechanism D: compare fsync count, latency and CPU at (N, T) = (1, 1 s), (64, 10 s) and (64, 60 s).
- N and T are compile-time `#define`s, and the flush thread checks only once a second ([src/storage_server.c:26](src/storage_server.c#L26)), so N = 1 can't mean one fsync per record, and the N = 64 trigger can be up to 1 s late.

  - **The flusher is woken at N:** between its 1 s passes, `gt_flusher_run` waits in the new `gt_storage_wait_due` on a condition variable (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC` on Linux) instead of sleeping. The append that makes a flush due wakes it, so N = 1 is one fsync per record and N = 64 is no longer up to 1 s late. T, rollover and the clock checks stay on the 1 s pass. ### PF-12: The verifier doesn't compare against the hub's sent `seq`s
- **DESIGN.md**, Test tooling: the verifier "then compares the log against the hub's sent-sequence log".
- `log_verify` checks every CRC, that `seq` strictly increases across segments, and that every hole is covered by a GAP, but there is no hub yet to compare against. Together with PF-03, a `kill -9` loss is currently undetectable.
- **Resolution (2026-10-27):**
  - **The rule:** compare ranges, not a per-`seq` log. Within one hub run the sent `seq`s are one unbroken range A..B: a `seq` is used only when `send()` succeeds, and a running hub's counter stays ahead of storage's reply (PF-03). A passing report already guarantees every `seq` from its first to its last is stored or GAP-covered, so:
    - lost = the sent `seq`s outside that range (`sent_seq_lost`);
    - a `seq` after B fails as `seq_not_sent`;
    - `seq`s before A are earlier hub runs and are allowed.
  - **Changed from the plan:** checking `data + gap_readings = B − A + 1` was dropped. It only held because `storage_feed` never sends a GAP. A hub GAP has its own `seq`, and its value counts refused readings that never got a `seq`, so the sum would break once the hub exists.
  - **The code:**
    - `gt_verify_sent` in `log_verify.h` / `log_verify.c`, written test first (VSR-01 to VSR-07 in `tests/test_verify_sent.c`).
    - `log_verify [--sent A..B] DIR` prints `sent=N lost=L` and fails on a mismatch.
    - `storage_faults.sh`'s settle check uses it in place of the bash arithmetic. It still checks N = B − A + 1 (no `seq` reused) and that the log starts at A, since its log starts empty.
  - **Docs:** DESIGN.md *Test tooling → Verifier*; Sensor-Pipeline.md's Mechanism D Code map, a Decisions bullet, the `VSR` prefix and the settle-check description.
  - **Tests:** `make test`, `make asan` and `make memcheck` all pass with VSR included (2026-10-27).
  - **Still to do:**
    - Record a `storage_faults.sh sigterm` / `kill9` run with the new check.

### PF-20
- **`.corrupt` files:** retention never deletes them, a second `.corrupt` of the same name silently replaces the first (`renameat`), and once the directory holds 128 names (`GT_FILE_LIST_MAX`), `gt_storage_open` fails.
- **Rollover failure logs every second:** while a new segment can't be created, `segment_create_error` is logged on every 1 s tick.
- **The 1970 file:** a Pi that boots with no network time and an empty log writes `log-19700101.bin` until NTP syncs (acknowledged in Lucas's *Not done yet*).
- **Resolution (2026-10-27):**
  - **Unique `.corrupt` names:** a second `.corrupt` copy of the same segment no longer replaces the first. Recovery picks the first free name of `<name>.corrupt`, `<name>.2.corrupt` … `<name>.99.corrupt` (SRV-12). Every name still ends in `.corrupt`, so `log_verify` counts them.
  - **Retention and the 128-name limit:** `.corrupt` files are still never deleted (decided 2026-10-27: they are evidence). The limit is now documented in `storage.h` and DESIGN.md: more than 128 names stops storage at start with `storage_open_error`, and the fix is to clear old `.corrupt` files by hand.
  - **`segment_create_error`:** it is now logged once per failure spell, and the next successful rollover re-arms it (FTK-12).
  - **The 1970 file (decided 2026-10-27):** on an empty log with an unsynced clock, `storage_main` now waits up to 120 s for the clock before open names the first segment. It logs `clock_wait max_s=120`, then `clock_wait_done waited_s=N synced=0|1`. The hub's 1024-record queue covers the wait. "Empty log" comes from the new `gt_storage_log_empty` / `_ops`, which uses the same listing open uses (SOP-16, red then green).
  - **Still possible:** with no network for the whole 120 s, it still starts a 1970 file. That stays a documented limit in `storage.h` and DESIGN.md.
  - **Not tested yet:** the wait itself has not been seen running, because WSL's clock is always synced. It needs a check on the Pi with the network unplugged.
  - **Doc follow-up (2026-10-27):** Sensor-Pipeline.md's *Not done yet (Mechanism D)* still listed "the 1970 file" as unfixed, saying a proper fix meant `storage_main` waiting for the clock. That wait now exists, so the bullet was reworded to the open item: the on-Pi check of the clock wait.

## What meets the plans

**DESIGN.md**
- **`storage_main.c` start-up order:** the one-listener lock, then recovery, then bind `storage.sock`, then the flush thread, then the rx loop. A second copy refuses to start.
- **Shutdown:** on SIGTERM, storage takes any records already in the socket, joins the flush thread, does the final flush, and writes the clean-shutdown marker only if that flush succeeded. The stop signals are blocked in the flush thread, SIGPIPE is ignored, and the exit status is honest. Seen working in the PF-04 run.
- **Recovery:** marker check, newest-segment header check and `.corrupt` rename, scan to the first bad record (magic, type, version, CRC, `seq`, partial tail), truncate + fsync, then the walk back for the last `seq`.
- **Durability:** fsync per batch; directory fsync when a segment is created; on a failed write or fsync the batch stays pending, storage is marked degraded, and the next cycle truncates to the last committed offset before rewriting.
- **Backlog and refusals:** `storage_backlog` at 50/75/90%; when full, refuse and count while still reading the socket; the next accepted record brings a GAP whose `seq` is the first refused reading.
- **Retention:** 30 days, deleting only outside the window and beyond the newest 30 segments; skipped while the clock is unsynced.
- **Locking:** the mutex is never held during file I/O.
- **Documentation brought in line:** the single pending buffer and memory budget, the commit sequence, recovery step 5, the retention rule, `storage.sock` as `SOCK_SEQPACKET`, and the `seq_resume` layout.
- **Verifier:** read-only, checks `seq` order across segment boundaries, its GAP rule matches what append writes, and it counts `.corrupt` files without failing on them (VFY, 10 tests).
- **Logging:** every line goes through `gt_log_format` with µs wall-clock timestamps.

**Sensor-Pipeline.md**
- **Lock helper:** the one-listener lock moved into a shared `src/` helper (`listen_sock.c`) with `fork()`-based tests (LCK), exactly as *Decisions* planned. `hub_listen` behaves as before.
- **Hop 2:** the 24 B record is checked with `gt_record_decode` and appended as the raw bytes received, per the 2026-10-23 decision. A storage GAP uses `sensor_id 0`, which the wire-format section allows.
- **Wrong-length frames:** storage receives into a 25 B buffer and closes the connection on a wrong length (`ipc_bad_message`), mirroring the hub's 17 B rule.
- **Same patterns:** events returned rather than logged, time passed in, a file seam with a fake for tests, `MSG_NOSIGNAL`, `SOCK_SEQPACKET`.
- **Test ID prefixes:** none of the 23 new prefixes collide with the existing ones.

Update Sensor-Pipeline.md's *Decisions* and `include/hub.h` to match.~~ **Done in both documents (2026-10-26).** `include/hub.h` waits for the hub steps.
2. ~~**Fix PF-04** (and PF-05), then run `storage_faults.sh sigterm 20` and `kill9 50` and record the results.~~ **Done (2026-10-26):** both ran with 0 failed checks; results are in PF-04/05 and the Mechanism D Status table.
3. ~~**Fix or document PF-06 and PF-07.**~~ **Done (2026-10-26):** both fixed test-first; see their Resolution lines.

No other process writes to the log. See the *Architecture Diagram* (storage subgraph) and *Mechanism mapping → Mechanism D*. 182 183 ### What is stored 184 185 The log holds two kinds of fixed-size record: 186 187 - **DATA record:** one accepted reading from one sensor. It holds the sensor ID, the hub-assigned sequence number, a timestamp and the sensor's **raw count**: 188 - Light (BH1750): raw 16-bit count. Lux = count / 1.2, converted when the data is read. 189 - Soil (STEMMA seesaw): raw capacitance count, roughly 200–2000. 190 191 Light and soil are stored as separate records, not combined into one row. Raw counts are stored rather than converted units, so calibration can change later without rewriting history. 192 - **GAP record:** an explicit marker that readings were refused. It holds the affected sensor, the gap's start time and the number of refused readings. The component that refuses the readings writes the gap record (sensor ring, hub queue or storage queue). See the rule above the *Failure-mode table*. 193 194 Readings that fail validation (out of range, or a malformed message) are rejected by the hub and are **not** stored. See the *Failure-mode table → Hub* rows. 195 196 The timestamp is applied by the hub when it receives the reading. If the Pi booted without network time, the timestamps may be wrong until NTP syncs. Ordering always comes from `seq`. See the *Failure-mode table → System clock*. 197 198 ### At what rate 199 200 | Stream | Rate | Records/day | 201 |---|---|---| 202 | Light | 1 per second | 86,400 | 203 | Soil | 1 per 60 s | 1,440 | 204 | **Total into storage** | **≈1.02 records/s (≈25 B/s)** | **87,840 ≈ 2.1 MB/day** | 205 206 On the wire, each reading travels sensor → hub as a 16 B socket message (layout under *In what format*). Hub → storage carries the 24 B record itself, laid out exactly as on disk with the CRC included: the hub stamps the timestamp when the reading arrives and `seq` + CRC when it sends the record, and storage checks the magic, version, type, sensor and CRC before appending it. On disk, each reading is one 24 B record. Gap records only appear during failures and add negligible volume. See the *Architecture Diagram* data path labels. 207 208 ### In what format 209 210 The log is an **append-only binary log** of fixed 24 B records, packed and little-endian. 211 212 **Segment header** (16 B, written once at the start of each file): 213 214 | Field | Size | Value | 215 |---|---|---| 216 | magic | 4 B | `"GTLG"` | 217 | version | 2 B | 1 | 218 | record_size | 2 B | 24 | 219 | created_at | 8 B | µs since the Unix epoch | 220 221 **Record** (24 B): 222 223 | Field | Size | DATA record | GAP record | 224 |---|---|---|---| 225 | magic | 1 B | `0xA7` | `0xA7` | 226 | record_type | 1 B | `0x01` | `0x02` | 227 | version | 1 B | 1 | 1 | 228 | sensor_id | 1 B | 1 = light, 2 = soil | affected sensor (0 = all) | 229 | seq | 4 B | hub sequence number | see below | 230 | timestamp | 8 B | hub receive time, µs since epoch | gap start, µs since epoch | 231 | value | 4 B | raw sensor count (u32) | refused-reading count (u32) | 232 | crc32 | 4 B | CRC-32 over bytes 0–19 | CRC-32 over bytes 0–19 | 233 234 - A gap ends at the timestamp of the next DATA record for the same sensor, so it needs no separate end field. 235 - Every record has a `seq`, and `seq` is strictly increasing across the log: 236 - Gaps created by a sensor or by the hub receive a hub-assigned `seq`. 237 - Gaps created by storage use the `seq` of the first refused reading. Their timestamp is that of the last record storage accepted before the gap: the earliest moment the gap could have started, since the missing readings' own times are lost with them. After a restart, recovery supplies it from the newest record on disk. A storage gap (`sensor_id` 0) ends at the next record of any sensor. 238 - Any record with an unknown `record_type` is treated as corrupt. 239 240 **Storage → hub `seq_resume` reply** (8 B, little-endian, defined in `include/storage_proto.h`), sent once as soon as the hub connects to `storage.sock`: 241 242 | Offset | Size | Field | Value | 243 |---|---|---|---| 244 | 0 | 1 B | magic | `0xA8` (distinct from the message's `0xA6` and the record's `0xA7`) | 245 | 1 | 1 B | version | 1 | 246 | 2 | 1 B | type | `0x10` seq_resume | 247 | 3 | 1 B | has_last | 0 = storage holds nothing yet (a fresh hub starts at 0; a running hub keeps its counter); 1 = `seq` is valid | 248 | 4 | 4 B | seq | the last accepted `seq` (0 when `has_last` is 0) | 249 250 - No CRC: the local socket keeps each message whole and does not corrupt it in transit; the record's CRC guards the SD card. 251 252 **Sensor → hub message** (16 B, packed and little-endian, defined in `include/ipc.h`): 253 254 | Offset | Size | Field | Value | 255 |---|---|---|---| 256 | 0 | 1 B | magic | `0xA6` (distinct from the record's `0xA7`) | 257 | 1 | 1 B | version | 1 | 258 | 2 | 1 B | type | `0x01` DATA, `0x02` GAP (same values as `record_type`) | 259 | 3 | 1 B | sensor_id | 1 = light, 2 = soil (0 is not valid from a sensor) | 260 | 4 | 4 B | counter | sensor-side counter; GAP: first refused reading | 261 | 8 | 4 B | seq | 0 from the sensor; the hub stamps it | 262 | 12 | 4 B | value | DATA: raw count; GAP: refused-reading count | 263 264 - The hub rejects a message with a bad magic, version, type or sensor_id (`ipc_bad_message`). A message shorter than 16 B is rejected at `recv()`. 265 - **Decided:** hub → storage sends the 24 B record (see *Record* above), not this message. The hub stamps the µs timestamp (8 B), which does not fit in 16 B alongside the type, sensor, seq and value. Stamping in the hub also keeps a record's receive time correct while it waits in the hub queue during a storage outage. 266 267 ### How records are organized 268 269 - There is one segment file per UTC day: `/var/lib/plantpi/log-YYYYMMDD.bin`. 270 - At midnight, storage first flushes the records it is holding into the old day's file, then creates the new one. A record goes into the previous day's file only if it arrived between midnight and the flush thread's next pass (≤ 1 s). 271 - Records are appended in `seq` order. Only the current day's file is open for writing, so only its tail can ever need recovery. 272 - When a new segment is created, storage fsyncs the directory as well, so the new file cannot disappear after a power cut. 273 274 ### With what retention 275 276 - Segments are kept for **30 days** (today and the 29 days before it), about 63 MB. When a new day's segment is created, a segment is deleted only if **both** its date is before that window **and** it is not one of the newest 30 segments. The second rule means a clock that jumps years ahead can't wipe out the history: retention only ever trims beyond 30 files. Rollover and retention are skipped while the clock is unsynced (`retention_skipped`, logged once per unsynced spell). 277 - **Nothing inside the 30-day window is ever deleted to make room.** If the card fills before 30 days (**planned**; until then a full card shows as `storage_write_error` (or `fsync_error`) + `storage_degraded`, with the records kept in memory): 278 - Storage logs `storage_disk_full`. 279 - It refuses and counts new readings. 280 - It writes a GAP record once space is available again. 281 - **Planned:** a 64 KB reserve (checked with `statvfs`) is always kept free, so a GAP record can always be written. 282 283 This follows the project's policy: protect existing history, and make any unavoidable loss explicit. See *Failure-mode table → Storage (disk full)*. 284 285 ### How writes are batched and when data is flushed 286 287 - The **rx thread** reads records from `storage.sock` and appends them, as the raw 24 B it received, to one **pending buffer** (up to 1 MB, about 43,690 records) under a mutex. The same buffer is the batch in normal operation and the outage queue when flushes fail, because records stay in it until a flush succeeds. 288 - The **flush thread** wakes once a second and commits when either of these comes first: 289 - **N = 64 records** pending, or 290 - **T = 60 s** since the **oldest** pending record was added (each record keeps its own add time, so a record that arrived during a slow flush still meets the 62 s commit target). At about 1.02 records/s, T is normally the trigger, which gives about 61 records (≈1.5 KB) per batch and about 1,440 fsyncs/day. 291 - **N and T are run-time options:** `storage_main -n N -t T_SECONDS` (default 64 and 60 s; N up to the 43,690-record buffer, T up to a day), logged on `storage_start` as `batch_n` / `batch_t_s`. The (N, T) comparison in *Mechanism D* therefore runs on one build. 292 - **N is acted on at once:** between its 1 s passes, the flush thread sleeps on a condition variable rather than a plain timer. The append that makes a flush due by count wakes it, so the commit starts straight away, and N = 1 really is one fsync per record. T, rollover and retention are still checked on the 1 s pass. The wake happens only when a flush *becomes* due: after a failed flush the records stay pending, and the thread retries on its next 1 s pass instead of spinning on a broken card. 293 - **Commit sequence:** 294 1. Lock the mutex and copy every pending record out (nothing is removed yet). 295 2. Unlock. The lock is never held during I/O. 296 3. `write()` them. 297 4. `fsync()` the segment. 298 5. Lock, drop the committed records from the buffer, record the new committed offset, unlock. 299 - **On SIGTERM**, storage commits whatever is pending, then creates the clean-shutdown marker `clean_shutdown` and fsyncs the directory. The marker is written only if that final flush succeeded. 300 - **A record is committed once `fsync()` returns.** Before then, it may be lost but is never reported as stored. 301 - **If `write()` or `fsync()` fails:** 302 - The batch stays in memory and storage is marked degraded immediately. 303 - On the next cycle, storage truncates the file back to the last committed offset, then rewrites and fsyncs the batch, so no duplicate or partial records reach the log. 304 - While the disk is unavailable, records keep queueing in the pending buffer, up to 1 MB (about 11 h). Storage logs `storage_backlog` once at each of 50%, 75% and 90% going up, with the threshold and the fill (`percent=N pending=P`). 305 - When the buffer is full, storage refuses and counts new readings (`storage_degraded reason=queue_full`, once per full spell). The next accepted reading skips their `seq`s, so a GAP whose `seq` is the first refused reading and whose count is the number refused goes in just before it. The GAP is stamped with the time of the last reading storage accepted before the refusals. 306 307 See *Mechanism D* (batching, durability point and outage rows) and *Failure-mode table → Storage*. 308 309 ### What happens when the power dies mid-write 310 311 **Guarantee:** a power cut loses at most one unsynced batch (≤ 60 s), plus any backlog held in memory during a storage outage. It never leaves a corrupt record readable. 312 313 On every start, **recovery runs before `storage.sock` accepts any data**. This is the same path after a power cut and after a supervisor restart or `kill -9`. Storage first takes the one-listener lock (`storage.sock.lock`), so no second storage process can be recovering or appending at the same time. 314 315 1. If the clean-shutdown marker `clean_shutdown` is missing and at least one segment exists, log `unclean_shutdown` (a fresh install has nothing to recover, so it is not reported). A marker that is there is deleted and the directory fsynced at once, so it can't survive into a run that later crashes. 316 2. Check the **newest** segment's header (only the segment being appended to can have a damaged tail). If it is invalid or the file is shorter than 16 B, rename it to `.corrupt`, log `segment_corrupt`, and start a fresh segment. An earlier `.corrupt` copy of the same segment is never replaced: the next copy becomes `.2.corrupt`, then `.3.corrupt`, and so on. `.corrupt` files are evidence and are never deleted. Known limit: storage reads at most 128 directory names, so a directory holding more (about 90 `.corrupt` files beside 30 segments) stops storage at start with `storage_open_error` until old `.corrupt` files are cleared by hand. 317 3. Scan the records from the start of the segment. Stop at the **first** record that has any of these problems: 318 - bad magic, unknown `record_type` or wrong version 319 - CRC mismatch 320 - `seq` that does not increase 321 - a partial (fewer than 24 B) trailing record 322 4. `ftruncate()` the file at that offset, `fsync()` it, and log `recovery_event` with the bytes and records removed. 323 5. If the newest segment holds no records (header-only, or renamed `.corrupt`), read older segments, newest first, until one gives the last `seq` on disk. Each older segment is recovered the same way, and every one that is cut or renamed is logged too (`recovery_event` / `segment_corrupt`, with its name). 324 6. Open `storage.sock` and resume normal operation. 325 326 Records are fixed-size, so the scan is simple offset arithmetic. The target is under 1 s for a full day's segment. 327 328 See *Mechanism D → "Survive being unplugged" and "Restarts must not corrupt the log"*, and *Failure-mode table → Storage (corrupt tail)* and *Power*. 329 330 ## Constraints and substitutions 331 This section covers compute, storage and IPC. No other process writes to the log. See the *Architecture Diagram* (storage subgraph) and *Mechanism mapping → Mechanism D*. ### What is stored The log holds two kinds of fixed-size record: - **DATA record:** one accepted reading from one sensor. It holds the sensor ID, the hub-assigned sequence number, a timestamp and the sensor's **raw count**: - Light (BH1750): raw 16-bit count. Lux = count / 1.2, converted when the data is read. - Soil (STEMMA seesaw): raw capacitance count, roughly 200–2000. Light and soil are stored as separate records, not combined into one row. Raw counts are stored rather than converted units, so calibration can change later without rewriting history. - **GAP record:** an explicit marker that readings were refused. It holds the affected sensor, the gap's start time and the number of refused readings. The component that refuses the readings writes the gap record (sensor ring, hub queue or storage queue). See the rule above the *Failure-mode table*. Readings that fail validation (out of range, or a malformed message) are rejected by the hub and are **not** stored. See the *Failure-mode table → Hub* rows. The timestamp is applied by the hub when it receives the reading. If the Pi booted without network time, the timestamps may be wrong until NTP syncs. Ordering always comes from `seq`. See the *Failure-mode table → System clock*. ### At what rate | Stream | Rate | Records/day | |---|---|---| | Light | 1 per second | 86,400 | | Soil | 1 per 60 s | 1,440 | | **Total into storage** | **≈1.02 records/s (≈25 B/s)** | **87,840 ≈ 2.1 MB/day** | On the wire, each reading travels sensor → hub as a 16 B socket message (layout under *In what format*). Hub → storage carries the 24 B record itself, laid out exactly as on disk with the CRC included: the hub stamps the timestamp when the reading arrives and `seq` + CRC when it sends the record, and storage checks the magic, version, type, sensor and CRC before appending it. On disk, each reading is one 24 B record. Gap records only appear during failures and add negligible volume. See the *Architecture Diagram* data path labels. ### In what format The log is an **append-only binary log** of fixed 24 B records, packed and little-endian. **Segment header** (16 B, written once at the start of each file): | Field | Size | Value | |---|---|---| | magic | 4 B | `"GTLG"` | | version | 2 B | 1 | | record_size | 2 B | 24 | | created_at | 8 B | µs since the Unix epoch | **Record** (24 B): | Field | Size | DATA record | GAP record | |---|---|---|---| | magic | 1 B | `0xA7` | `0xA7` | | record_type | 1 B | `0x01` | `0x02` | | version | 1 B | 1 | 1 | | sensor_id | 1 B | 1 = light, 2 = soil | affected sensor (0 = all) | | seq | 4 B | hub sequence number | see below | | timestamp | 8 B | hub receive time, µs since epoch | gap start, µs since epoch | | value | 4 B | raw sensor count (u32) | refused-reading count (u32) | | crc32 | 4 B | CRC-32 over bytes 0–19 | CRC-32 over bytes 0–19 | - A gap ends at the timestamp of the next DATA record for the same sensor, so it needs no separate end field. - Every record has a `seq`, and `seq` is strictly increasing across the log: - Gaps created by a sensor or by the hub receive a hub-assigned `seq`. - Gaps created by storage use the `seq` of the first refused reading. Their timestamp is that of the last record storage accepted before the gap: the earliest moment the gap could have started, since the missing readings' own times are lost with them. After a restart, recovery supplies it from the newest record on disk. A storage gap (`sensor_id` 0) ends at the next record of any sensor. - Any record with an unknown `record_type` is treated as corrupt. **Storage → hub `seq_resume` reply** (8 B, little-endian, defined in `include/storage_proto.h`), sent once as soon as the hub connects to `storage.sock`: | Offset | Size | Field | Value | |---|---|---|---| | 0 | 1 B | magic | `0xA8` (distinct from the message's `0xA6` and the record's `0xA7`) | | 1 | 1 B | version | 1 | | 2 | 1 B | type | `0x10` seq_resume | | 3 | 1 B | has_last | 0 = storage holds nothing yet (a fresh hub starts at 0; a running hub keeps its counter); 1 = `seq` is valid | | 4 | 4 B | seq | the last accepted `seq` (0 when `has_last` is 0) | - No CRC: the local socket keeps each message whole and does not corrupt it in transit; the record's CRC guards the SD card. **Sensor → hub message** (16 B, packed and little-endian, defined in `include/ipc.h`): | Offset | Size | Field | Value | |---|---|---|---| | 0 | 1 B | magic | `0xA6` (distinct from the record's `0xA7`) | | 1 | 1 B | version | 1 | | 2 | 1 B | type | `0x01` DATA, `0x02` GAP (same values as `record_type`) | | 3 | 1 B | sensor_id | 1 = light, 2 = soil (0 is not valid from a sensor) | | 4 | 4 B | counter | sensor-side counter; GAP: first refused reading | | 8 | 4 B | seq | 0 from the sensor; the hub stamps it | | 12 | 4 B | value | DATA: raw count; GAP: refused-reading count | - The hub rejects a message with a bad magic, version, type or sensor_id (`ipc_bad_message`). A message shorter than 16 B is rejected at `recv()`. - **Decided:** hub → storage sends the 24 B record (see *Record* above), not this message. The hub stamps the µs timestamp (8 B), which does not fit in 16 B alongside the type, sensor, seq and value. Stamping in the hub also keeps a record's receive time correct while it waits in the hub queue during a storage outage. ### How records are organized - There is one segment file per UTC day: `/var/lib/plantpi/log-YYYYMMDD.bin`. - At midnight, storage first flushes the records it is holding into the old day's file, then creates the new one. A record goes into the previous day's file only if it arrived between midnight and the flush thread's next pass (≤ 1 s). - Records are appended in `seq` order. Only the current day's file is open for writing, so only its tail can ever need recovery. - When a new segment is created, storage fsyncs the directory as well, so the new file cannot disappear after a power cut. ### With what retention - Segments are kept for **30 days** (today and the 29 days before it), about 63 MB. When a new day's segment is created, a segment is deleted only if **both** its date is before that window **and** it is not one of the newest 30 segments. The second rule means a clock that jumps years ahead can't wipe out the history: retention only ever trims beyond 30 files. Rollover and retention are skipped while the clock is unsynced (`retention_skipped`, logged once per unsynced spell). - **Nothing inside the 30-day window is ever deleted to make room.** If the card fills before 30 days (**planned**; until then a full card shows as `storage_write_error` (or `fsync_error`) + `storage_degraded`, with the records kept in memory): - Storage logs `storage_disk_full`. - It refuses and counts new readings. - It writes a GAP record once space is available again. - **Planned:** a 64 KB reserve (checked with `statvfs`) is always kept free, so a GAP record can always be written. This follows the project's policy: protect existing history, and make any unavoidable loss explicit. See *Failure-mode table → Storage (disk full)*. ### How writes are batched and when data is flushed - The **rx thread** reads records from `storage.sock` and appends them, as the raw 24 B it received, to one **pending buffer** (up to 1 MB, about 43,690 records) under a mutex. The same buffer is the batch in normal operation and the outage queue when flushes fail, because records stay in it until a flush succeeds. - The **flush thread** wakes once a second and commits when either of these comes first: - **N = 64 records** pending, or - **T = 60 s** since the **oldest** pending record was added (each record keeps its own add time, so a record that arrived during a slow flush still meets the 62 s commit target). At about 1.02 records/s, T is normally the trigger, which gives about 61 records (≈1.5 KB) per batch and about 1,440 fsyncs/day. - **N and T are run-time options:** `storage_main -n N -t T_SECONDS` (default 64 and 60 s; N up to the 43,690-record buffer, T up to a day), logged on `storage_start` as `batch_n` / `batch_t_s`. The (N, T) comparison in *Mechanism D* therefore runs on one build. - **N is acted on at once:** between its 1 s passes, the flush thread sleeps on a condition variable rather than a plain timer. The append that makes a flush due by count wakes it, so the commit starts straight away, and N = 1 really is one fsync per record. T, rollover and retention are still checked on the 1 s pass. The wake happens only when a flush *becomes* due: after a failed flush the records stay pending, and the thread retries on its next 1 s pass instead of spinning on a broken card. - **Commit sequence:** 1. Lock the mutex and copy every pending record out (nothing is removed yet). 2. Unlock. The lock is never held during I/O. 3. `write()` them. 4. `fsync()` the segment. 5. Lock, drop the committed records from the buffer, record the new committed offset, unlock. - **On SIGTERM**, storage commits whatever is pending, then creates the clean-shutdown marker `clean_shutdown` and fsyncs the directory. The marker is written only if that final flush succeeded. - **A record is committed once `fsync()` returns.** Before then, it may be lost but is never reported as stored. - **If `write()` or `fsync()` fails:** - The batch stays in memory and storage is marked degraded immediately. - On the next cycle, storage truncates the file back to the last committed offset, then rewrites and fsyncs the batch, so no duplicate or partial records reach the log. - While the disk is unavailable, records keep queueing in the pending buffer, up to 1 MB (about 11 h). Storage logs `storage_backlog` once at each of 50%, 75% and 90% going up, with the threshold and the fill (`percent=N pending=P`). - When the buffer is full, storage refuses and counts new readings (`storage_degraded reason=queue_full`, once per full spell). The next accepted reading skips their `seq`s, so a GAP whose `seq` is the first refused reading and whose count is the number refused goes in just before it. The GAP is stamped with the time of the last reading storage accepted before the refusals. See *Mechanism D* (batching, durability point and outage rows) and *Failure-mode table → Storage*. ### What happens when the power dies mid-write **Guarantee:** a power cut loses at most one unsynced batch (≤ 60 s), plus any backlog held in memory during a storage outage. It never leaves a corrupt record readable. On every start, **recovery runs before `storage.sock` accepts any data**. This is the same path after a power cut and after a supervisor restart or `kill -9`. Storage first takes the one-listener lock (`storage.sock.lock`), so no second storage process can be recovering or appending at the same time. 1. If the clean-shutdown marker `clean_shutdown` is missing and at least one segment exists, log `unclean_shutdown` (a fresh install has nothing to recover, so it is not reported). A marker that is there is deleted and the directory fsynced at once, so it can't survive into a run that later crashes. 2. Check the **newest** segment's header (only the segment being appended to can have a damaged tail). If it is invalid or the file is shorter than 16 B, rename it to `.corrupt`, log `segment_corrupt`, and start a fresh segment. An earlier `.corrupt` copy of the same segment is never replaced: the next copy becomes `.2.corrupt`, then `.3.corrupt`, and so on. `.corrupt` files are evidence and are never deleted. Known limit: storage reads at most 128 directory names, so a directory holding more (about 90 `.corrupt` files beside 30 segments) stops storage at start with `storage_open_error` until old `.corrupt` files are cleared by hand. 3. Scan the records from the start of the segment. Stop at the **first** record that has any of these problems: - bad magic, unknown `record_type` or wrong version - CRC mismatch - `seq` that does not increase - a partial (fewer than 24 B) trailing record 4. `ftruncate()` the file at that offset, `fsync()` it, and log `recovery_event` with the bytes and records removed. 5. If the newest segment holds no records (header-only, or renamed `.corrupt`), read older segments, newest first, until one gives the last `seq` on disk. Each older segment is recovered the same way, and every one that is cut or renamed is logged too (`recovery_event` / `segment_corrupt`, with its name). 6. Open `storage.sock` and resume normal operation. Records are fixed-size, so the scan is simple offset arithmetic. The target is under 1 s for a full day's segment. See *Mechanism D → "Survive being unplugged" and "Restarts must not corrupt the log"*, and *Failure-mode table → Storage (corrupt tail)* and *Power*. ## Constraints and substitutions This section covers compute, storage and IPC. Stress 3 reports the headroom and is not pass/fail. | Step | Rate | Target | |---|---|---| | Baseline | 1× (≈1 record/s) | No backlog; ≈1,440 fsyncs/day | | Stress 1 | 10× (≈10 records/s) | No backlog; fsync p99 within baseline range | | Stress 2 | 100× (≈100 records/s) | **No backlog growth over 10 min** | | Stress 3 | Ramp until the backlog grows | Report the ceiling; aim ≥ 1,000 records/s (informational) | We also compare fsync count, write latency and CPU at (N, T) = (1, 1 s), (64, 10 s) and (64, 60 s), as committed in *Mechanism D*, by starting `storage_main` with `-n` / `-t` (see *How writes are batched*). ### CPU usage | Measurement | Method | Target | |---|---|---| | CPU time per process (utime + stime) | Sample `/proc//stat` every 10 s during the 72 h soak and during each stress step | < 2% of one core in total at the real load | | SoC temperature and throttling | `vcgencmd measure_temp` and `vcgencmd get_throttled` every 60 s during the soak | No throttling events (see *Constraints → Pi CPU / RAM*) | ### Memory usage The goal is to show the system stays stable over the 72 h soak, not to hit an absolute size. | Measurement | Method | Target | |---|---|---| | Leaks | Valgrind memcheck on short runs of each process | 0 bytes definitely or indirectly lost | | Growth | Sample `VmRSS` / `VmHWM` from `/proc//status` every 60 s over 72 h | Flat after warm-up; no upward trend in any process | | Buffer bounds | Each buffer logs its high-water mark; a forced storage outage fills the storage pending buffer | No buffer ever exceeds its cap (sensor ring 64, hub queue 1024, storage pending buffer 1 MB). 1 # Sensor Pipeline: plan and status 2 3 The official plan for Green Thumb's sensor-side pipeline, from the I2C seam up to the 16 B message a sensor process sends to the hub and the 24 B record the hub sends to storage. That covers the BH1750 light-sensor driver and the shared pieces it relies on: sensor health tracking, the log line formatter, the sensor→hub message and the hub→storage record codec, plus the IPC client that carries the 16 B message over `hub.sock`. A new session should be able to read this file, plus `CLAUDE.md` and `DESIGN.md`, and pick up where work stopped without re-explanation. 4 5 Since 2026-10-26 the file also holds a second top-level part, *Mechanism D: storage*, with its own Goal, Code map, Decisions, Status, *Not done yet* and Log. So there are two Status sections: **Status** (the sensor pipeline and IPC, Steps 0–24) and **Status (Mechanism D)** (storage). **Update either Status section only at the end of the day, when asked.** 6 7 ## Context 8 - **Owner:** Lily (DESIGN.md → Ownership map: "Light sensor (driver and process)" and "IPC (data path)"). 9 - **Goal of this phase:** prove the sensor is *electrically alive* and *trustworthy* before it is connected to the data pipeline. That means the bus opens, the chip ACKs, reads decode, failures are retried and bounded, and a sensor that keeps failing is marked offline instead of silently producing nothing. Then pin the wire message the light process will send. 10 - **Goal of the IPC phase (Steps 10–24):** a reading leaves the sensor process and reaches a hub stand-in (`hub_listen`) over `hub.sock`. It survives the hub being killed and restarted (buffered, then resent in order, or covered by a GAP), and the client never blocks the 1 Hz sampling. 11 - **Hardware:** BH1750 on `/dev/i2c-1` at address `0x23` (ADDR pin low or floating). Continuous high-res mode at 1 lx/count; each conversion takes at most 180 ms. Lux = raw / 1.2. **Raw counts are stored, never lux.** 12 - **Sampling rate:** 1 Hz (DESIGN.md). The 1 Hz schedule belongs to the sampler, not the driver. 13 - **Rule from DESIGN.md's failure-mode table (Sensor (I2C) row):** retry 3× at 10 ms, then skip the sample. After 10 consecutive failures, mark the sensor offline and retry every 5 s. Log `i2c_read_error`, `sensor_offline` and `sensor_online`. 14 15 ## Design principle 16 - **Layered seam:** `src/i2c_bus.c` is the only file that makes I2C system calls. The driver talks to the bus only through `gt_i2c_ops` (`write` / `read` / `sleep_ms` / `close`). Tests swap in `tests/fake_i2c.h`, so every driver path, including injected NACKs and short reads, runs in WSL/CI with no hardware. 17 - **Logic stays separate from hardware** (CLAUDE.md): anything that can be pure logic (health tracking, message encoding) takes its inputs as arguments (`gt_status`, `now_ms`, bytes) and makes no system calls. 18 - **Each layer fails explicitly:** a failure returns a `gt_status` and leaves outputs untouched. No layer invents a value. 19 - **IPC seam (same idea as the I2C seam):** `src/ipc_sock.c` is the only file that makes **client-side** socket system calls (`socket`, `connect`, `send`, `close`). Servers make their own (see *Decisions*, PF-16). The IPC client (`src/ipc_client.c`) talks to the socket only through `gt_sock_ops` (`connect` / `send` / `disconnect` / `destroy`), with the current time passed in as `now_ms`. Tests swap in `tests/fake_sock.h`, so the backoff, ring and GAP logic all run in WSL/CI with no hub and no real waiting. 20 21 ### Code map 22 How the modules work together to carry a reading from sensor → IPC → hub → storage. Legend: ✅ done · ☐ later. The IPC phase (Steps 10–24) is complete; `hub_listen` stands in for the hub until `hub.c` exists. The storage process is built (*Mechanism D: storage* at the end of this file has its own, more detailed code map). 23 24 ```mermaid 25 flowchart LR 26 subgraph SENSOR["light_sensor process · light_sensor_main.c ☐ (soil process: same shape, Lucas)"] 27 SMP["sampler ☐

**Who calls whom (one row per arrow):** 57 58 | Caller | Callee | Passes | Returns | 59 |---|---|---|---| 60 | sensor main loop | `gt_sampler_tick` | `now_ms` | — | 61 | sampler | `gt_light_read` | — then `gt_record_encode` | the queued record, stamped with `next_seq` just before `send()` | 24 B → `storage.sock` | 70 | `storage_main` | `gt_storage_open` (wraps `gt_storage_open_ops` with the Linux `now_ms` (decoded and checked inside, stored unchanged) | OK / CORRUPT / FULL + event flags | 72 | storage flush thread (`gt_flusher_tick`) | `gt_storage_rollover`, then `gt_storage_flush` | `now_us`, `now_ms`, clock synced | write + fsync of the pending batch, event flags | 73 74 ### The "electrically alive" ladder 75 Each rung can only be checked once the rung below it passes. `light_probe` prints rungs 1–4 as a PASS/FAIL checklist on the Pi. 76 77 | Rung | What it proves | Where it's checked | Detected by | 78 |---|---|---|---| 79 | 1 | The I2C bus device opens (I2C enabled, permissions OK) | `light_probe` check 1; LSO-02 | `open()` fails → ENOENT / EACCES hint | 80 | 2 | A BH1750 ACKs at 0x23 (wiring, ADDR pin, power) | `light_probe` check 2; LSO-03/04 | First write (POWER_ON) is NACKed | 81 | 3 | One measurement reads and decodes | `light_probe` check 3; LSR-01..03 | 2-byte read, high byte first | 82 | 4 | Sampling holds 1 Hz with p99 jitter < 10 ms | `light_probe` check 4 | `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` deviation from an absolute schedule | 83 | 5 | A sensor that keeps failing is marked offline, probed every 5 s, and announced when it comes back | **Steps 1–3 (health tracker + log line)** | 10 consecutive failed reads | 84 85 ### Open: what each failure point has acquired, and what must be unwound 86 `gt_light_open_bus` takes ownership of the bus, so the caller never cleans up: 87 88 | Fails at | Acquired so far | Unwound | Returns | 89 |---|---|---|---| 90 | `bus.ops == NULL` | nothing | nothing | `NULL` | 91 | `malloc` of driver state | the bus | `bus.ops->close` | `NULL` | 92 | POWER_ON / RESET / CONT_HRES write | bus + state | close the bus once, `free(s)`, no settle wait | `NULL` | 93 | after CONT_HRES | — | waits 180 ms so the first read returns real data | handle | 94 95 ### Read: budget 96 In the worst case a read makes 1 try + 3 retries with 3 × 10 ms gaps, so it waits 30 ms, far inside the 1 s period. On failure the function returns `GT_ERR_IO` with `raw_out` untouched, so the caller skips the sample (LSR-07). The same handle works again after an outage, with no reopen (LSR-09). 97 98 ## Decisions 99 - **The health tracker is generic** (`sensor_health`), not light-only, so the soil process can reuse it. It is a small public struct with no malloc. 100 - **Health input:** any non-`GT_OK` result from `gt_light_read` counts as one failure. The driver's 3 retries are already inside a single failed read. 101 - **Health output:** `gt_health_record` returns a transition event (`NONE` / `OFFLINE` / `ONLINE`) and the caller logs it. The tracker does no I/O. 102 - **Time is passed in** as `now_ms`, matching `gt_sampler_tick`, so tests need no clock. 103 - **Test ID prefixes:** `SHR` (sensor health record), `SHS` (sensor health should-read), `SHE` (sensor health event name), `LGF` (log format), `MSE` (message encode), `MSD` (message decode), `CRC` (CRC-32), `RCE` (record encode), `RCD` (record decode), `IFD` (IPC frame decode), `ICO` (IPC client open), `ICC` (IPC client close), `ICS` (IPC client send), `ICR` (IPC client reconnect), `IOV` (IPC client overflow), `IPL` (IPC loopback over a real socket). 104 - **Log ownership:** the light sensor's events (`i2c_read_error`, `sensor_offline`, `sensor_online`) are Lily's, as the light process's read-failure handling. The shared formatter (`gt_log_format`) has no owner in the Ownership map because every component uses it, so it counts as **Joint → Architecture integration**. Lily writes it first, as its first caller; give Lucas a heads-up so his components reuse it. 105 - **Log line:** ` [ key=value ...]`. The timestamp is µs since the Unix epoch, as a plain integer, the same unit as the on-disk record, so logs and records can be joined. The levels are `DEBUG` / `INFO` / `WARN` / `ERROR`. The light process logs `sensor_offline` as WARN and `sensor_online` as INFO. 106 - **Log sink: stderr** (decided 2026-10-27, PF-18). The formatter only fills a caller-provided buffer, and every process writes the finished `gt_log_format` line to stderr, as `storage_main` already does. Children inherit the supervisor's stderr, so under systemd every line lands in the journal. Each process still reads the wall clock for its own timestamps. A shared file sink was rejected (rotation becomes our problem), and so was sending lines to the monitor process (it waits on Mechanism E). 107 - **Hop 2 (hub→storage) carries the 24 B on-disk record** (decided 2026-10-23). The hub stamps `seq` and the µs timestamp, builds the record (CRC included), and storage checks it (amended 2026-10-26, PF-01: the timestamp is stamped on arrival, `seq` + CRC at send time; see *Hub contract (hop 2)*) with `gt_record_decode`, then appends it unchanged. There are two reasons. First, DESIGN.md already has the hub stamping the time and storage reading *records* from `storage.sock`. Second, a record that waits in the hub's 1024-record queue during a storage outage (up to about 17 min) keeps its real receive time. If storage stamped the time instead, the timestamp would be off by however long the record waited. 108 - **The hub's next `seq` after connecting to storage is max(own next, `seq_resume` + 1)** (decided 2026-10-26, PF-03). A freshly started hub has no counter, so it takes storage's reply + 1 (0 on an empty log). A running hub keeps its own counter, defined as 1 + the last `seq` whose `send()` succeeded, so records storage lost in a `kill -9` (unsynced, or still in the socket) leave a hole that storage turns into a GAP (`recovery_gap`). The alternative, always continuing from the reply, was rejected: it reuses the lost `seq`s, so the loss leaves no GAP and the hub's sent log holds duplicates, which breaks "no reading is lost silently" and the Evaluation plan's lost-readings formula. Only a loss where the hub restarts too (power cut) is shown by `unclean_shutdown` alone, which DESIGN.md's Power row already allows. Storage needed no change: its sequence guard already writes the GAP. This rule sets what PF-01 (when to stamp) and PF-02 (the sender's states) must support, and what `storage_faults.sh` checks (PF-04/05). 109 - **Hub contract for hop 2** (decided 2026-10-26, PF-01/PF-02): the hub stamps the time on arrival and `seq` + CRC at send; the socket seam gains `recv`; the sender waits for `seq_resume` (2 s deadline) before sending anything. See *Hub contract (hop 2)*. 110 - **Message magic is `0xA6`** (proposed), distinct from the on-disk record's `0xA7`, so a record can never be misread as a message. 111 - **Truncated messages are rejected at `recv()`,** which must return exactly `GT_MSG_SIZE`, not in decode. Decode keeps its fixed 16 B array. 112 - **Range checks stay in the hub:** decode doesn't check that light ≤ 65535. That is the hub's `reading_invalid` check. 113 - **Deferred:** `src/light_sensor_main.c` (open → sample → health → send) waited until the IPC client existed. The client was completed on 2026-10-24, so it is now the next item (see *Not done yet*). 114 - **`hub.sock` is AF_UNIX `SOCK_SEQPACKET`** (decided 2026-10-24). The kernel keeps message boundaries, so each `send()` is one whole 16 B message and each `recv()` returns exactly one message. A short message shows up as a short `recv()`, which is where DESIGN.md rejects it, and there are no partial sends to track. `SOCK_STREAM` would need frame reassembly and resync code in the hub. 115 - **`hub_listen` stands in for the hub on the Pi** (decided 2026-10-24) until `gt_hub_accept` and the hub process exist. It's a small tool (`src/hub_listen_main.c`, `make hub_listen`) that prints each decoded message and flags counter gaps. With it, the kill -9 / kill -STOP fault tests can run now. 116 - **The client never blocks the sampler:** every socket call is non-blocking, and `send` uses `MSG_NOSIGNAL`, so a dead hub returns `EPIPE` instead of raising SIGPIPE, which would kill the sensor process. 117 - **Time is passed in** (`now_ms` on `gt_ipc_client_send` / `_pump`), as with the health tracker, so the backoff tests need no clock and no sleeps. 118 - **Events are returned, not logged:** the client returns `GT_IPC_EV_DISCONNECT` / `_RECONNECT` / `_OVERFLOW` bit flags, and the caller logs `ipc_disconnect` / `ipc_reconnect` / `ipc_overflow`, the same pattern as `gt_health_record`. 119 - **`gt_ipc_client_open` doesn't connect.** A hub that isn't up yet is not an error (DESIGN.md, Mechanism E: processes tolerate unavailable peers at startup). The first attempt happens on the first send or pump. 120 - **GAP needs 2 free slots:** after an overflow, a new reading is accepted only when the ring can hold both the GAP and the reading. This keeps the order: old data, then the GAP, then new data. Otherwise the reading is refused and counted into the same gap. 121 - **Close drops the buffer:** `gt_ipc_client_close` sends nothing more. Readings still in the ring are lost, and that's documented, not silent. 122 - **Limitation (no app-level ack):** a message the kernel accepted but the hub never `recv()`d before dying is lost. The hub sees the jump in the counter as a `sensor_seq_gap`. 123 - **`gt_ipc_client_open_ops` is declared in `ipc_sock.h`, not `ipc.h`** (Step 11). `ipc_sock.h` includes `ipc.h`, so putting it in `ipc.h` would make the two headers include each other. `gt_light_open_bus` sits next to its seam in `light_sensor.h` for the same reason. 124 - **Ownership of the ctx:** once `ops` is non-NULL, the client owns the ctx and calls `destroy` exactly once, from `close` or straight away if the client can't be allocated. With NULL ops there's no `destroy` to call, so the caller keeps the ctx. 125 - **`send` drains, pushes, then drains again** (Step 18). Draining before the push sends older frames first, which can free the slot the new reading needs, so a reading isn't refused when the hub could already have taken the backlog. 126 - **Any send result other than OK or FULL counts as the hub gone** (Step 19): disconnect, report `GT_IPC_EV_DISCONNECT` and retry after the wait. Both failure paths (a failed connect and a lost hub) share `schedule_retry`, so the wait doubles the same way for each. 127 - **Order moved to fit the link** (decided 2026-10-24). Every test binary links every file in `src/`, so nothing in `src/` may call a function that doesn't exist yet. `gt_ipc_client_open` calls `gt_ipc_sock_linux`, so it moved from Step 16 to Step 22, and its tests ICO-03/04 moved from Step 15 to Step 21. ICC-03 needs `send` to leave a frame in the ring, so it moved from Step 17 to Step 18. 128 - **One listener per socket, enforced by a lock** (decided 2026-10-24). A process that listens on a socket (`hub_listen` now; the hub and storage later) first takes an `fcntl` write lock on `.lock` and holds it for its whole life. Only the lock holder may remove a leftover socket file and bind a new one; a second copy prints `already running` and exits without touching anything. The kernel drops the lock when the holder dies, `kill -9` included, so a crash never leaves a stale lock. This is safer than probing with `connect()`, which leaves a gap: two copies started together could both see the file as stale, and the second would take the first one's address. Closing *any* fd the process holds on the lock file releases the lock, so the file is opened in one place only. When the hub is written, this moves into a shared `src/` helper; testing it needs `fork()`, because a process never blocks on its own `fcntl` lock. 129 - **The socket seam is for clients; servers call the socket API directly** (decided 2026-10-27, PF-16). Clients (`gt_ipc_client`, and later the hub's hop-2 sender) go through `gt_sock_ops`, because their backoff, ring and resume logic is worth testing against a fake with no real waiting. Servers (`listen_sock.c`, `storage_server.c`, and later the hub's rx loop) call `socket` / `bind` / `listen` / `accept` / `recv` / `send` themselves and are tested over real sockets in a `/tmp` directory (LBD, SSV, and later the hub loopback). A server loop is mostly "wait in `poll()`, then hand the bytes on", which a real socket tests well. A server-side seam with its own fake was rejected: it would add an ops table and a second fake to test very little logic. 130 131 ## Wire format: sensor → hub message (16 B, little-endian, encoded byte by byte) 132 | Off | Size | Field | Value | 133 |---|---|---|---| 134 | 0 | 1 | magic | `GT_MSG_MAGIC` = `0xA6` | 135 | 1 | 1 | version | `GT_MSG_VERSION` = 1 | 136 | 2 | 1 | type | `GT_MSG_DATA` = 1, `GT_MSG_GAP` = 2 (same values as `gt_rec_type`) | 137 | 3 | 1 | sensor_id | 1 light, 2 soil (0 = all is not valid on hop 1) | 138 | 4 | 4 | counter | sensor-side counter (for a GAP: the first refused counter) | 139 | 8 | 4 | seq | 0 from the sensor; the hub stamps it | 140 | 12 | 4 | value | DATA: raw count; GAP: refused-reading count | 141 142 Magic and version are written by encode and checked by decode. They are not `gt_msg` fields; `type` becomes one. 143 144 ## Wire format: hub → storage record (24 B) 145 Hop 2 sends the on-disk record exactly as DESIGN.md *In what format → Record* lays it out: magic `0xA7`, type, version, sensor_id, seq (u32 at 4), timestamp (u64 µs at 8), value (u32 at 16) and CRC-32 over bytes 0–19 (at 20). `gt_record` and the codec live in `include/log_record.h`. **Watch the header order:** the record goes magic, **type, version**, sensor_id, while the message goes magic, **version, type**, sensor_id. Don't copy the message encoder without swapping those two bytes. Unlike the message, a GAP record may use sensor_id 0 (all). 146 147 ## Hub contract (hop 2): stamping, numbering and the sender 148 Decided 2026-10-26 to settle PF-01 and PF-02 (Pipeline-Findings.md) before any hub code exists. It builds on the PF-03 numbering rule in *Decisions*. Nothing here is built yet. `include/hub.h` and `include/ipc_sock.h` change to match when the hub steps start, test first. 149 150 **Why it changes (PF-01):** a hub that has just started doesn't know its next `seq` until storage's `seq_resume` reply arrives. Storage may be down or still recovering, and Mechanism E says the hub must keep running anyway. So the hub can't finish a record (`seq` + CRC) when the sensor message arrives. It finishes it when it sends it. 151 152 ### Who stamps what, and when 153 | Field | Set by | When | Why | 154 |---|---|---|---| 155 | `type`, `sensor_id`, `value` | `gt_hub_accept` | message arrives | copied from the checked message | 156 | `timestamp_us` | `gt_hub_accept` (`now_us` passed in) | message arrives | keeps the real receive time while the record waits in the queue (the 2026-10-23 reason still holds) | 157 | `seq` | the hop-2 sender | just before `send()` | only the sender knows the next `seq` (max rule) | 158 | CRC-32 | `gt_record_encode`, called by the sender | just before `send()` | the CRC covers `seq`, so it can't be computed earlier | 159 160 - **`gt_hub_accept`'s new contract:** validate, range-check and de-duplicate one `gt_msg`. On `GT_OK`, fill `*out` with type, sensor, value and `timestamp_us = now_us`, and leave `seq` at 0. The hub plan adds the event flags it returns (`reading_invalid`, `ipc_duplicate`, `sensor_seq_gap`). They're outside this contract. 161 - **The queue holds unstamped `gt_record`s:** 1024 slots of the in-memory struct (24 B with padding), so DESIGN.md's "1024 records × 24 B" budget still holds. A queued record has no `seq` and no CRC yet. 162 - **A `seq` is used only when `send()` returns `GT_OK`.** The sender stamps the queue head with `next_seq` and encodes it. On OK it drops the record and adds 1 to `next_seq`. On FULL or IO the record stays at the head, unchanged, and `next_seq` doesn't move, so a failed send never makes a hole in the numbering. 163 164 ### The max rule, shared 165 - **`gt_next_seq`** (pure, in `include/storage_proto.h` next to `gt_resume`, because it says what the reply means): `gt_status gt_next_seq(int has_own, uint32_t own_next, const gt_resume *resume, uint32_t *next_out)`. It sets `*next_out` to max(`own_next`, `resume->seq` + 1). With `has_own` 0 (a fresh sender) it uses `resume->seq` + 1, or 0 when `resume->has_last` is 0. `GT_ERR_INVAL` for NULL arguments; `GT_ERR_FULL` when the reply's `seq` is `UINT32_MAX` (no next `seq` exists); `*next_out` is untouched on failure. Built and tested 2026-10-26 (NSQ 8/8). 166 - **Both callers use it:** the hop-2 sender and `storage_feed` (PF-04/05; `storage_feed` done 2026-10-26). The fault rounds then test the same numbering code the hub runs. `storage_proto.c` is Mechanism D's file, so give Lucas a heads-up. 167 168 ### The socket seam gains `recv` (PF-02) 169 `gt_sock_ops` adds one op. The sensor client never calls it, but `src/ipc_sock.c` and `tests/fake_sock.h` both implement it: 170 ```c 171 /* Receive one whole message into buf (cap bytes). Non-blocking. 172 * GT_OK with *len_out = the message length, or *len_out = 0 when nothing 173 * is waiting (EAGAIN); GT_ERR_IO when the peer closed (recv returns 0) or 174 * reset the connection. */ 175 gt_status (*recv)(void *ctx, uint8_t *buf, size_t cap, size_t *len_out); 176 ``` 177 - **The sender reads into `GT_RESUME_SIZE + 1` bytes**, like the storage and hub receivers, so an oversized reply shows up as too long. 178 - **`tests/fake_sock.h` grows:** scripted `recv` replies (bytes, "nothing yet", or IO), and its `sent` frames sized to 24 B as well as 16 B (they are fixed at `GT_MSG_SIZE` today). 179 - `gt_ipc_sock_linux(path)` already takes any path and sends any length, so it serves `storage.sock` unchanged apart from `recv`. 180 181 ### Sender state machine (`include/hub_sender.h`, `src/hub_sender.c`) 182 ``` 183 connect() OK → resume_deadline = now + 2000 ms 184 DISCONNECTED ─────────────────────────────────────────────▶ AWAITING_RESUME 185 ▲ attempt only when now ≥ next_attempt │ recv nothing yet → stay (until the deadline) 186 │ backoff 100 ms → 2 s, as the client │ valid 8 B reply → gt_next_seq → SENDING 187 │◀── deadline passes, or a bad / wrong-size reply ─────────────┤ 188 │ (ipc_bad_message), or recv IO: disconnect, retry later │ 189 │ ▼ 190 └──── send IO (EPIPE / ECONNRESET): head record kept ───── SENDING: drain oldest first, 191 unstamped, storage_unreachable once stamp seq + encode + send; 192 FULL → stop, stay connected 193 ``` 194 - **Nothing is sent before the reply.** In AWAITING_RESUME, records only queue. This is the state the plan's two-state client lacks. 195 - **No call ever blocks:** the reply is polled with `recv` from `pump`, and a reply that never comes ends at the 2 s deadline (the same 2 s `storage_feed` waits). After that the sender disconnects and retries with backoff. 196 - **Own counter:** `has_own` becomes 1 after the first successful send in this process and stays 1 across reconnects. That's what lets storage see a `kill -9` loss as a hole (PF-03). 197 - **Storage sends nothing after the reply.** Anything received in SENDING is `ipc_bad_message`: disconnect and reconnect. 198 - **Events are returned as flags** (`storage_unreachable`, `storage_reconnected`, `hub_queue_full`), and the hub logs them, as `gt_ipc_client` does. 199 - **Queue full (`hub_queue_full`):** refuse and count, as the client ring does. The GAP needs 2 free slots, and the order is old records, then the GAP, then new ones. The GAP is `{type GAP, sensor_id 0, timestamp_us = the first refused reading's receive time, value = refused count}`, and it gets its `seq` at send like any other record. 200 - **API shape:** `gt_hub_sender_open_ops(ops, ctx)` (doesn't connect; owns the ctx as the client does), `gt_hub_sender_push(sender, const gt_record *unstamped, now_ms)` → OK / FULL / INVAL, `gt_hub_sender_pump(sender, now_ms)` → event flags, `gt_hub_sender_close`, and a stats getter (queued, refused, `next_seq`, `has_own`). 201 202 ### Test prefixes (reserved; none collide with the existing ones) 203 `NSQ` next seq (fresh, running, empty log, reply ahead of the counter, NULL), `HAC` hub accept (fields, `seq` left 0, timestamp), `HSO` sender open/close, `HSR` resume wait (deadline, bad reply, IO, nothing sent before the reply), `HSS` sending (stamp on OK only, FULL keeps the head, IO keeps the head, the counter survives a reconnect), `HSQ` queue full and GAP, `HSL` loopback against `gt_storage_serve` over a real socket (a storage restart in the middle leaves a GAP for a running sender and none after a SIGTERM). 204 205 ### Follow-ups this contract creates 206 - **DESIGN.md:** done 2026-10-26. The Hub → storage rows, the hub-queue budget and *At what rate* now say a record gets its `seq` + CRC when it is sent. 207 - **`include/hub.h`:** rewrite the `gt_hub_accept` comment to match (with the hub steps, not now). 208 209 ## Health state machine 210 ``` 211 10th consecutive failure → EV_OFFLINE, next_probe = now + 5000 212 ONLINE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ OFFLINE 213 ▲ success → reset count │ should_read() true only when now ≥ next_probe 214 │ failure → count++ (no event before 10) │ failed probe → EV_NONE, next_probe = now + 5000 215 └────────────────────── success → EV_ONLINE, count = 0 ◀─────┘ 216 ``` 217 218 ## IPC client: connection and ring rules 219 ``` 220 connect() OK → wait = 100 ms 221 (EV_RECONNECT only if a disconnect or failed attempt came before) 222 DISCONNECTED ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ CONNECTED 223 ▲ attempt only when now ≥ next_attempt │ drain ring oldest first: 224 │ connect() fails → next_attempt = now + wait, │ send OK → drop frame, keep going 225 │ wait = min(wait × 2, 2000 ms) │ send FULL → stop (EAGAIN), stay connected 226 └──── send IO (EPIPE / ECONNRESET) → EV_DISCONNECT once, frame kept, ◀┘ 227 next_attempt = now + wait 228 ``` 229 - **Starting state:** the client starts DISCONNECTED with `next_attempt = 0`, so the first send or pump tries to connect straight away. A clean first connect fires no event. 230 - **Backoff:** the waits run 100 → 200 → 400 → 800 → 1600 → 2000 ms, then stay at 2000 ms, so attempts fall at 0, 100, 300, 700, 1500, 3100, 5100 ms… Any successful connect resets the wait to 100 ms. 231 - **Ring:** 64 slots × 16 B (≈1 KB, DESIGN.md resource budget). Each message is encoded when it enters the ring, so a bad message is rejected (`GT_ERR_INVAL`) before it takes a slot. Frames leave only when `send` returns OK. 232 - **What `send` returns to the caller:** 233 - `GT_OK`: the message was sent or buffered. 234 - `GT_ERR_FULL`: it was refused and counted. 235 - `GT_ERR_INVAL`: bad arguments or a bad message. 236 237 A disconnect is not an error to the caller: it is reported through the event flags. 238 - **Overflow:** 239 - **Ring full:** the new reading is refused, `refused` goes up by one, and the client remembers the first refused counter. `EV_OVERFLOW` fires once per overflow run, not once per refusal. 240 - **Gap pending:** the next reading is accepted only when **2 slots** are free. The client then enqueues the GAP `{type = GAP, sensor_id, counter = first refused, value = refused count}`, followed by the reading. With fewer than 2 free slots, the reading is refused into the same gap. 241 - **Order on the wire:** the buffered old data, then the GAP, then the new data. 242 - **`pump`:** does the same connect-and-drain as `send` without a new message. The sensor loop calls it every tick, so the ring still drains while the sensor is offline and not producing readings. 243 - **Close:** sends nothing and calls `destroy` once. Buffered frames are dropped. 244 245 ## Steps 246 **Workflow** (CLAUDE.md and the user's preferences): 247 - One step per turn. Stop after each step for review; the user commits. 248 - Each write the user approves is at most a file skeleton plus one method, and ideally just one method (one test case counts as one method).
